Mars and Venus still may have their differences, but better computer technology might just help level the playing field in at least one area. While research has found that men generally do better with map reading and finding their way around unfamiliar territory due to a slight evolutionary edge in spatial relations, a new study has shown that women can wend their way through simulated 3-D computer environments just as well as men can when given a larger field of view and smoother animation.

The study was conducted by Desney S. Tan, who is pursuing a doctorate at the school of computer science at Carnegie Mellon University, and Mary Czerwinski and George G. Robertson, computer researchers for Microsoft. For this recent test, the scientists used a 43-inch wide curved display screen and put 11 men and 11 women through computer-generated 3-D mazes similar to those found in the video game Doom.

Optical flow, the relative motion of stationary objects going by a moving person, proved to be a big factor separating men and women. Choppy animation generally made it harder for the women in the test to get their bearings in the maze. With smooth, realistic animation on a wide screen, though, the women were able to match the men's ability to navigate through a virtual environment.

Mr. Tan said he and his colleagues were seeking ways to influence productivity in more typical computing tasks. ''We know women do a lot of things fundamentally different from men, so we're very careful with that,'' he said. ''We want to make sure we design for the entire population.''

The Russian oil giant Yukos and the government continued a standoff on Thursday over the fate of a controlling stake in the company, Russia's largest exporter.

On Wednesday, a deadline passed for Yukos to pay $3.4 billion in back taxes for 2000. That day, court bailiffs, backed by the paramilitary police, raided an office that keeps the main registry of Yukos shareholders -- potentially a guide to which assets to seize.

Yukos is said to be in off-again, on-again talks with the government on a possible settlement. A deal could mean that Mikhail B. Khodorkovsky, the main shareholder and former chief executive of Yukos, would surrender his stake, possibly in exchange for an extension to pay Yukos's mounting tax debts. Without it, Yukos has said it cannot pay; its bank accounts are frozen and it is barred from selling assets. Mr. Khodorkovksy's trial on charges of tax evasion and fraud resumes on Monday.

Russia's president, meanwhile, played host to the leader of Germany on Thursday and offered investment assurances. ''The most persuasive signal for investment today is Russia's macroeconomic situation,'' President Vladimir V. Putin said during a visit by Chancellor Gerhard Schröder.

Mr. Schröder said German business leaders did not view the government's actions against Yukos as a threat to their business. ''I can understand that a government that has a right to collect tax also wants to collect it,'' Mr. Schröder said, according to news agencies. ''It's an internal Russian affair. There's no lack of confidence between German and Russian companies.''

Since the end of World War II, Democrats and Republicans have alternated control of the Pennsylvania governor's office, switching every eight years. If that pattern holds next year, the current Republican incumbent, Gov. Tom Ridge, who is limited to two four-year terms, will be succeeded by a Democrat.

And the pattern is likely to hold, some Republican leaders have begun to grumble.

As they see it, not one of the contenders for the Republican nomination has the political heft to beat either of the Democratic hopefuls.

Not one of the worried Republican leaders has publicly voiced concern about the trio -- Attorney General Mike Fisher, State Treasurer Barbara Hafer and State Senator Jeffrey E. Piccola -- but some are said to be casting about for a candidate who strikes them as having a better shot at beating the Democratic nominee, Edward G. Rendell, a former Philadelphia mayor and former general chairman of the Democratic National Committee, or Robert P. Casey Jr., the state auditor general and son of former Gov. Robert P. Casey.

Initially, Republicans had high hopes that Lt. Gov. Mark Schweiker would be their nominee. They figured that with his name recognition and the help of Governor Ridge's network of party workers and fund-raisers, he would be able to break the state's half-century pattern of changing party stripes in the governor's office every eight years. But Mr. Schweiker decided he would rather spend more time with his family.

The effort to broaden the field of Republican hopefuls has gone nowhere. So the likelihood is that Mr. Fisher will get the nomination, in good part because Governor Ridge has indicated he may endorse him.

And the Democratic nominee?

That contest looks to be close (and divisive, Republicans hope).

Mr. Rendell has more money but Mr. Casey is probably better known statewide and probably has a better state organization.

Senator Harry Reid of Nevada, the Democratic leader in the Senate, issued an apology on Thursday to 33 of his Republican colleagues. The apology came after a document, distributed by Reid's office, listed campaign contributions that some of the Republicans had received from the lobbyist Jack Abramoff, along with critical news reports on their past actions and statements.

The document, which was distributed on Wednesday, contained a list of 33 Senators, including some of the most prominent names in the Republican party, such as Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and former presidential candidate Ted Cruz. The document also highlighted contributions that some of these Senators had received from Abramoff, who was convicted in 2006 on charges of fraud, conspiracy, and tax evasion in connection with his lobbying activities.

Reid's apology came after several Republican Senators expressed their outrage at the document's contents. They argued that the document was an attempt to smear their reputations and to imply that they were somehow involved in Abramoff's criminal activities. Some Senators also questioned the timing of the document's release, noting that it came just days before the Senate is scheduled to vote on a major campaign finance reform bill.

In his apology, Reid acknowledged that the document was "inappropriate and unacceptable," adding that it was "not the way to conduct the people's business." He also said that he had instructed his staff to remove the document from the Senate's website and to refrain from distributing any similar materials in the future.

Reid's apology, however, did little to quell the anger of some of his Republican colleagues. Senator John Thune of South Dakota, who was also named in the document, called the apology "insufficient" and said that Reid should "personally apologize to each and every Senator who was targeted in this inappropriate and unacceptable document."

Senator Susan Collins of Maine, another Senator named in the document, said that she was "disappointed" by Reid's actions and that she would "expect more from the leader of the Senate." She also called on Reid to "take responsibility for his actions and to ensure that this kind of thing does not happen again in the future."

The controversy surrounding the document comes at a time when the Senate is deeply divided along partisan lines, with Democrats and Republicans frequently clashing over key issues such as healthcare, immigration, and taxes. It remains to be seen whether Reid's apology will help to ease these tensions, or whether it will simply serve to further inflame them.

In the meantime, the Senate is set to vote on the campaign finance reform bill in the coming days. The bill, which was introduced by Democrats, aims to increase transparency in political donations and to curb the influence of special interest groups in the electoral process. While the bill is expected to face stiff opposition from Republicans, it is unclear whether the controversy surrounding Reid's document will have any impact on the outcome of the vote.

The semiconductor industry is set to break records this year, according to the nation's leading semiconductor trade group. The group said on Wednesday that chip sales would reach an all-time high as the economy continues to improve and demand for personal computers and cellphones continues to grow.

The rise in demand for electronic devices is a result of the pandemic, which has forced people to work and study from home. As a result, the demand for laptops, tablets, and smartphones has skyrocketed. This has led to an increase in demand for semiconductor chips, which are used in the production of these devices.

The semiconductor industry has had a difficult year due to the pandemic, with many factories shutting down production due to supply chain disruptions and a decrease in demand. However, the industry has rebounded strongly, with many companies reporting record profits in the last quarter.

The trade group said that the growth in the semiconductor industry would continue in the coming years, driven by the rise in demand for electric vehicles, artificial intelligence, and the Internet of Things. These technologies require advanced semiconductor chips, which are becoming increasingly important in modern society.

The semiconductor industry is a vital part of the global economy, with many countries investing heavily in the development of this technology. The United States, China, and South Korea are among the top producers of semiconductor chips, with many companies operating in these countries.

The rise in demand for semiconductor chips has also led to an increase in the price of these components. This has led to concerns that the cost of electronic devices could rise in the coming months, as manufacturers pass on the increased costs to consumers.

Despite these concerns, the trade group said that the semiconductor industry was well-positioned to meet the growing demand for chips. Many companies have invested heavily in the development of new manufacturing facilities, which will help to increase production and reduce costs.

In conclusion, the semiconductor industry is set to break records this year, driven by the rise in demand for electronic devices. The industry is a vital part of the global economy and is expected to continue to grow in the coming years, driven by the rise in demand for advanced technologies. While there are concerns about the rising cost of semiconductor chips, the industry is well-positioned to meet the growing demand for these components.

The Russian oil company Yukos and the government are still at odds over the fate of a controlling stake in the corporation, which is the largest exporter in Russia. The standoff has been ongoing for some time now, and tensions between the two sides are high.

The government claims that Yukos owes a large sum of money in back taxes and has seized the company's assets as a result. Yukos, on the other hand, says that the government is simply trying to take control of the company for political reasons.

The situation has become increasingly complicated in recent days, with both sides refusing to back down. The government has threatened to sell off Yukos' assets to pay the back taxes, while Yukos has warned that such a move would be illegal and could lead to a major international incident.

Despite the tension, both sides have expressed a willingness to negotiate and find a solution to the problem. However, it is unclear how long this standoff will continue, or what the eventual outcome will be.

For now, the fate of Yukos remains uncertain, and the future of Russia's largest exporter hangs in the balance. Many are watching the situation closely, hoping for a peaceful resolution that will benefit both sides and avoid any further escalation of the conflict.

Reuters, the news service and data company, which is trying to meet stringent cost-cutting targets, said Thursday it would triple the number of employees it has in India by the end of next year.

As many as 1,500 employees, or a tenth of the company's total, will be in Bangalore by 2006, company executives said during a ceremony to open a building in southern India. Reuters already has 340 employees in Bangalore, including about 13 journalists. The company said it planned to move mainly data and technical jobs to Bangalore. The editorial staff in Bangalore is expected to increase to 50 by early next year, Reuters told union representatives.

The company's chief executive, Tom Glocer, is embracing outsourcing to reduce costs. He foreshadowed Thursday's announcement in September at an investor conference.

''The amazing thing -- and this is the dirty little secret about outsourcing that people need to talk about publicly a bit more -- not only is the cost conflation amazing at four, five or even six to one, but the quality and productivity is better too,'' Mr. Glocer said in September. ''We are flooded. We have 100 qualified applications for every data input person and these people have qualified accounting degrees.''

The company, which now employs 1,000 data-processing workers at about 40 sites worldwide, plans to shift 450 jobs to Bangalore initially, mainly from Tiverton, England; White Plains, N.Y.; and Singapore.

Analysts said that action fits into the company's greater strategy. ''This doesn't surprise me at all, given the targets they have set for themselves,'' said Paul Sullivan, a media analyst at Merrill Lynch in London. Reuters has pledged to cut costs by £440 million ($782 million) by the end of 2006, and Mr. Sullivan said the number was considered ''sacrosanct.'' Reuters said Thursday that costs in Bangalore were about 40 percent lower than in New York or London.

The Bangalore office supplies information on companies and debt and equity issues. Later, it will also provide information on mergers, acquisitions and equity pricing.

Union leaders expressed concern about the move, which they said could impair the quality of news and data Reuters offers. ''We're talking about people halfway around the world from where the news is happening, in a different continent and time zone,'' said Peter Szekely, chairman of the Reuters unit of the Newspaper Guild of New York.

Reuters executives said that the plan would not result in job losses in the editorial division.

Mercury Air Group Inc., a Los Angeles-based aviation services company, has announced its intention to spin off and separately list its fuel sales and services unit by August 2001. This strategic move is expected to unlock the potential of both businesses and allow them to focus on their respective core operations.

The fuel sales and services unit, which is a key component of Mercury Air Group's overall business, has been witnessing steady growth in recent years. By spinning off and listing it separately, the company aims to capitalize on this growth and attract investors who are specifically interested in the fuel sales and services sector.

In addition to the spin-off, Mercury Air Group Inc. plans to continue expanding its aviation services offerings, which include aircraft maintenance, ground handling, and cargo services. The company believes that this expansion will lead to a stronger market position and increased profitability for both the aviation services and fuel sales and services divisions.

While the exact details of the spin-off have not been disclosed, the company has confirmed that the process will be completed by August 2001. Industry experts have praised the move, stating that it could potentially lead to a more focused and efficient business model for Mercury Air Group Inc.

Overall, this development is expected to have a positive impact on the company's performance and growth in the coming years. Investors and stakeholders in the aviation industry will be closely watching the progress of this spin-off and the subsequent listing of the fuel sales and services unit.

The Treasury has announced a limited number of auctions this week, with just two scheduled events. Today's sale will feature new three- and six-month bills, drawing the attention of investors and market watchers alike.

This decision comes as a surprise to many, as the Treasury typically holds a greater number of auctions throughout the week. The choice to limit the offerings may have significant consequences for both short- and long-term investors. The sale of these new bills could potentially influence the market, as well as the overall economy.

The three-month bills, which have a maturity date of just 90 days, are often considered a safe and reliable investment option. They typically offer lower returns than longer-term investments, but they provide a level of stability that can be appealing to more risk-averse investors. With a relatively short maturity period, these bills are often used as a means to park funds for a short period, while still earning a modest return.

On the other hand, the six-month bills offer a slightly longer investment horizon and may be more attractive to those seeking higher returns. These bills, with a maturity period of 180 days, often provide a higher yield than their three-month counterparts. As with any investment, however, the potential for higher returns comes with an increased level of risk. Investors must weigh the potential benefits against the inherent risks associated with a longer investment period.

The limited number of auctions this week may be indicative of the Treasury's attempt to gauge the market's appetite for these new bills. With only two auctions scheduled, it is likely that demand for these short-term investment options will be closely monitored by both the Treasury and investors.

This week's auction announcement has certainly piqued the interest of the financial community, as many are eager to see how the market reacts to the limited offerings. As the Treasury moves forward with the sale of these new three- and six-month bills, it remains to be seen what impact this decision will have on the broader economy.

In conclusion, the Treasury's announcement of only two auctions this week is a notable departure from its typical schedule. The sale of new three- and six-month bills today will likely attract a wide range of investors, all eager to capitalize on these short-term investment opportunities. As the market adjusts to this unexpected development, the outcome of this week's auctions could have far-reaching implications for both investors and the economy as a whole.

A consortium led by Haier, a large Chinese conglomerate, abandoned its $1.28 billion bid for the appliance maker Maytag late yesterday, according to people involved in the negotiations. Haier's decision to drop its bid came just two days after the Whirlpool Corporation made a $1.36 billion offer for Maytag.

The move ends the prospect of a three-way battle for Maytag. In May, the company agreed to be sold to Ripplewood Holdings, the private equity firm, for $1.13 billion, but Haier's unsolicited offer put it into play.

The decision by Haier, which was backed in its bid by the Blackstone Group and Bain Capital, may also temporarily calm some anxious nerves in Washington about the possibility of a second American corporate brand name falling into the hands of the Chinese.

Haier's bid came just as Cnooc, a Chinese-owned oil company, made a $18.5 billion offer for Unocal, stirring a spirited debate about United States economic ties to China.

People close to Haier suggested that it abandoned its offer after the group determined, once it reviewed Maytag's confidential records, that it would have to change some of its financial projections, and also that the group was not prepared for a takeover battle with Whirlpool.

Without Haier, the battle for control of Maytag is between Ripplewood and Whirlpool. Whirlpool has already clearly outbid Ripplewood, though its offer is a mix of stock and cash and may present some risk of being blocked by regulators because the combined company would dominate the home appliance industry.

There is some question whether Maytag is allowed to provide Whirlpool with its confidential records under its already agreed-upon deal with Ripplewood.

It is also unclear whether Ripplewood is prepared to raise its offer. Ripplewood at one point suggested that Maytag pay it a $40 million fee to terminate their deal while Maytag was engaged in talks with Haier.

Ripplewood will have five days to match Whirlpool's offer under the agreement the companies signed in May.

Peter Kent would seem a credible critic of the Canadian news media, with his history as an anchor for two of Canada's television networks and as a correspondent.

But when Mr. Kent recently sent a letter to journalism schools challenging them to formally examine his contention that Canadian journalists are biased against the Conservative Party of Canada, he himself was criticized. And the reason is that Mr. Kent, the deputy editor of Global Television News, is also a Conservative candidate in the next Canadian federal election.

In the letter he sent to the journalism schools last month and in an interview, Mr. Kent said, ''I don't take part in anything that involves content.''

Mr. Kent has been leading a double life as a TV news executive and political candidate for almost five months, and not everyone is comfortable with the arrangement. After a columnist in The Toronto Globe and Mail wrote about Mr. Kent's challenge to the journalism schools, Peter Desbarats, a former dean of the journalism school at the University of Western Ontario in London, responded with a letter.

''As far as I remember, journalists who have run for political office in the past have always resigned from their news or editorial positions,'' Mr. Desbarats, who is also a friend of Mr. Kent, wrote. ''If we're talking about journalistic objectivity, perhaps Peter Kent should start with his own case before making sweeping claims of bias against all other journalists and journalism educators.''

But Christopher Dornan, the director of the journalism school at Carleton University in Ottawa, and Paul Knox, his counterpart at Ryerson University in Toronto, said they were not concerned, provided that Mr. Kent stayed away from editorial decisions.

They were less supportive of his challenge for a study of media bias, however. Both said that smaller studies of the Canadian media suggested that the results might not be worth the trouble.

''The problem with the argument that most Canadian journalists are Liberals is that most Canadians are Liberals,'' Professor Knox said. ''You can criticize that situation for being the tyranny of the majority. But you can't criticize it for being unrepresentative.''

IAN AUSTEN

Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger Apologizes for Racially Insensitive Remarks

On Friday, Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger issued a public apology for racially insensitive remarks he made during a closed-door meeting in March. The former action movie star and current California governor said in the meeting that Cubans and Puerto Ricans were naturally passionate due to their combination of "black blood" and "Latino blood."

The comments, which have only recently come to light, have sparked outrage and criticism from various groups and individuals, particularly from the Cuban and Puerto Rican communities. The governor's remarks were seen as offensive and perpetuating harmful stereotypes about people of African and Latino descent.

In response to the backlash, Gov. Schwarzenegger took to social media to express his remorse for the comments. In a statement posted on Twitter, the governor wrote, "I apologize if my words offended anyone. I have always valued diversity and have worked hard to promote unity and understanding among all people."

The governor went on to explain that his comments were not intended to be derogatory or harmful, but rather a reflection of his own observations and experiences. "Throughout my life, I have met many people from different backgrounds and cultures," he wrote. "I have always been fascinated by the passion and energy that I have seen in the Cuban and Puerto Rican communities. My comments were meant to celebrate that passion, not to diminish or demean it."

Despite the governor's apology, the controversy surrounding his remarks has continued to grow. Several prominent politicians and civil rights activists have called for the governor to take further action to demonstrate his commitment to racial equity and sensitivity.

In an interview with local news outlet, Assemblywoman Carmen Arroyo, who is of Puerto Rican descent, said, "Gov. Schwarzenegger's apology is a good start, but he must do more to make amends for his harmful words. It's important for our leaders to recognize the impact that their words can have on entire communities."

Similarly, Cuban-American actor and activist Andy Garcia expressed his disappointment in the governor's remarks. "It's disheartening to hear someone in a position of power make such thoughtless comments," he said. "We must continue to push for greater understanding and respect for all people, regardless of their racial or ethnic background."

As the fallout from Gov. Schwarzenegger's comments continues, it remains to be seen what further action he will take to address the concerns of those offended by his remarks. However, his public apology serves as a reminder of the importance of careful and sensitive language when discussing matters of race and ethnicity.

Microsoft announced yesterday that it has hired Steven Berkowitz, the chief executive of Ask Jeeves, to lead its struggling Internet division. The move comes as the tech giant aims to revive its position in the highly competitive online market, which is currently dominated by companies like Google and Facebook.

Berkowitz, who has been the CEO of Ask Jeeves since 2001, will be responsible for managing and developing Microsoft's Internet business, which has been facing numerous challenges in recent years. The company's search engine, Bing, has been struggling to gain market share against Google, and its social networking efforts have not been as successful as those of its rivals.

Microsoft's Internet division has also been plagued by several high-profile departures, including Kevin Johnson, the former head of the division, who left the company in 2008. The hiring of Berkowitz is seen as an attempt by Microsoft to bring in fresh leadership and ideas to help turn around its online fortunes.

In a statement, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said, "We are excited to welcome Steven to the Microsoft family. His experience and leadership in the Internet industry will be invaluable as we work to improve our Internet offerings and better compete in this fast-growing market."

Berkowitz's appointment comes at a crucial time for Microsoft, as the company is in the midst of a major transformation under the leadership of Nadella. Since taking over as CEO in 2014, Nadella has been focusing on transitioning Microsoft from a primarily software-based company to one that is more focused on cloud computing and online services.

The company's Internet division is a key part of this strategy, as it includes products such as Bing, MSN, and the recently launched Microsoft Edge browser. However, despite significant investment in these areas, Microsoft has struggled to make significant inroads in the online market.

Berkowitz's experience at Ask Jeeves could prove invaluable in helping Microsoft to better compete in the search engine market. Ask Jeeves, which was founded in 1996, was once one of the most popular search engines on the Internet, but has since been overshadowed by the rise of Google.

During his tenure at Ask Jeeves, Berkowitz helped to guide the company through several major acquisitions and partnerships, including the purchase of search engine Teoma in 2001 and a partnership with Google in 2002. He also oversaw the company's rebranding as Ask.com in 2005 and its subsequent sale to IAC/InterActiveCorp in 2005.

It remains to be seen whether Berkowitz will be able to replicate his success at Ask Jeeves in his new role at Microsoft. However, his appointment is a clear signal that the tech giant is committed to reviving its Internet division and becoming a more formidable competitor in the online market.

As Microsoft continues to pivot towards a more cloud-centric business model, the success or failure of its Internet division under Berkowitz's leadership will likely have a significant impact on the company's overall performance and future prospects.

Egypt's largest Islamic opposition group, the Muslim Brotherhood, has doubled the number of seats its members will hold in Parliament, the state-run Middle East News Agency and members of the group said Wednesday, based on preliminary reports of vote totals from a runoff election on Tuesday.

The outlawed but tolerated group, whose members run as independents under the banner ''Islam Is the Solution,'' appears to have won 34 seats out of the 164 that were up for election in the first of three regional rounds of voting, posing a serious challenge to the ruling National Democratic Party, which appears to have won 70 seats.

A coalition of about nine secular parties, including Kifaya, or Enough, appeared to have won only 8 seats while independents won about 50.

The strong performance of the Muslim Brotherhood caused surprise in political and intellectual circles in Egypt. Members of the group said they were amazed.

''The election result reflects the political awareness of Egyptians,'' said Muhammad Akef, an official of the group, on its Web site. ''It also mirrors the high-level performance of the Muslim Brotherhood, who set a good example, in the election.''

During previous parliamentary election campaigns, the government has arrested the group's candidates, intimidated its potential voters and torn down its campaign banners. This time, candidates associated with the group were allowed to hold campaign rallies, hang banners and distribute their platforms.

Egypt had its first contested presidential election in September, which opened an unprecedented national debate on political reform and civil liberties. While political analysts attribute the better treatment of opposition candidates to a shift in President Hosni Mubarak's attitude toward reform, the legislative elections remain mainly dependent on the personalities of the candidates.

Muhammad Salah, Cairo bureau chief of the pan-Arab newspaper Al Hayat and an expert on Islamic groups, said the results reflected the division inside the governing National Democratic Party's so-called old guard and the new generation led by Gamal Mubarak, the president's son, and his policy committees.

''People are just sick and tired of the party's games, they just hate the way the party is run,'' Mr. Salah said.

In the current Parliament, the governing party controls about 405 of the 444 seats for which members are elected. (Ten are appointed by the president.) The rest of the seats will be contested in two coming rounds of voting.

Even if the Muslim Brotherhood does equally well in those elections, it is not expected to overturn the political system in Egypt.

In an ongoing battle between rival phone companies, a court-appointed arbitrator ruled yesterday that Gary D. Forsee is allowed to leave his position at BellSouth and take up the role of chief executive at Sprint. However, arbitrator William H. Webster has placed certain restrictions on what Mr. Forsee can do within his new position at the company.

This decision by the arbitrator brings an end to the protracted tug of war between the two rival phone companies, who have been embroiled in a legal dispute over the executive's move. BellSouth had previously maintained that Mr. Forsee's departure would result in the loss of trade secrets and confidential information, which would ultimately be detrimental to their business. Sprint, on the other hand, argued that Mr. Forsee was the ideal candidate for the role of chief executive and that his appointment would be crucial to the company's future success.

In his ruling, arbitrator William H. Webster acknowledged the concerns of both parties and attempted to strike a balance between their competing interests. While he allowed Mr. Forsee to make the move to Sprint, he also imposed certain restrictions on the executive's activities within his new role. These restrictions are designed to protect BellSouth's interests and prevent the potential misuse of sensitive information.

The specific details of the restrictions imposed on Mr. Forsee have not been made public, but it is expected that they will limit his involvement in certain strategic decisions and access to confidential information. This is likely to be a temporary measure, with the restrictions being lifted after a certain period of time has elapsed. Both Sprint and BellSouth have expressed their willingness to abide by the arbitrator's decision and are now looking forward to moving past this contentious issue.

The resolution of this dispute comes at a crucial time for both companies, as the telecommunications industry is currently facing significant challenges and undergoing rapid change. With Mr. Forsee's appointment now confirmed, Sprint is hoping that his leadership will help the company navigate these challenges and secure its position as a leading player in the market. BellSouth, on the other hand, will need to find a suitable replacement for the outgoing executive and ensure that their business remains competitive in the face of increasing pressure from rivals.

Overall, the decision by arbitrator William H. Webster represents a compromise between the competing interests of BellSouth and Sprint. While it allows Mr. Forsee to make the move to his new role at Sprint, it also seeks to protect the interests of BellSouth and prevent any potential harm to their business. It remains to be seen how these restrictions will impact Mr. Forsee's ability to lead Sprint effectively and whether the company will be able to overcome the challenges facing the telecommunications industry.

Lockheed Martin Corporation, a global aerospace and defense company, announced last night that it has entered into an agreement to acquire Titan Corporation for a staggering $1.8 billion. The deal, which will be paid in a combination of cash and stock, aims to expand Lockheed Martin's capabilities to handle more of the government's communications systems and information networks.

Titan Corporation, a provider of advanced technology solutions and services, has been a key player in the government communications industry for several years. Its expertise in information technology, satellite communications, and intelligence systems has made it a valuable asset for government agencies. The acquisition of Titan Corporation will allow Lockheed Martin to further strengthen its position in the sector and enhance the solutions it offers to its clients.

The deal is expected to be completed by the end of the year, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions. Upon completion, Titan Corporation will become a wholly-owned subsidiary of Lockheed Martin, and its operations will be integrated into the company's existing business structure.

The acquisition comes at a time when the demand for advanced communication systems and information networks has never been higher. As governments around the world continue to invest in modernizing their infrastructures, Lockheed Martin's move to acquire Titan Corporation is a strategic decision aimed at capitalizing on this growing market.

"This acquisition is a significant milestone for Lockheed Martin and a testament to our commitment to providing cutting-edge solutions to our clients," said a spokesperson for Lockheed Martin. "By combining our resources and expertise, we will be better equipped to meet the evolving needs of the government's communications systems and information networks."

The $1.8 billion deal is expected to have a positive impact on Lockheed Martin's financial performance. Analysts predict that the acquisition will contribute to the company's earnings growth and enhance shareholder value in the long run.

As Lockheed Martin continues to expand its operations and capabilities in the government communications sector, it is clear that the acquisition of Titan Corporation marks the beginning of a new chapter for the company. With the combined expertise of both organizations, Lockheed Martin is poised to become an even more formidable force in the industry, ensuring the security and efficiency of government communications systems and information networks for years to come.

Porter J. Goss, the director of the Central Intelligence Agency, delivered a long-awaited internal report to Congress on Monday night that is said to give a harsh assessment of the agency's performance before the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

Mr. Goss, who was chairman of the House Intelligence Committee before his appointment last year as head of the C.I.A., hand-delivered two copies of the classified report to staff members of the House and Senate Intelligence Committees.

The copies of the report, which is several hundred pages, were placed in committee safes and were not to be opened at least until Wednesday, said a Congressional official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak with the press on the record.

The report was prepared by the C.I.A.'s inspector general, John L. Helgerson, in response to a request in December 2002 from the joint Congressional inquiry into the attacks. By statute, Mr. Helgerson, who joined the C.I.A. in 1971 and became inspector general in 2002, is the agency's independent watchdog, reporting to Congress as well as to the agency.

A draft report was given to Mr. Goss in October, but he postponed its release so that people criticized for their role in the failure to prevent the 2001 attacks could review and respond to the accusations. Officials and former officials named in the report gave their responses to Mr. Helgerson before he completed the report in late June.

On July 22, Mr. Goss informed Congressional officials in a brief note that the final report had been completed.

The draft report was described by intelligence officials in January as highly critical of George J. Tenet, the former C.I.A. director, and James L. Pavitt, the former deputy director for operations, both of whom retired last year. A spokesman for Mr. Tenet, Bill Harlow, and Mr. Pavitt both took issue with the reported findings in interviews at that time.

Representative Jane Harman of California, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said she would favor asking the C.I.A. to declassify as much of the report as possible. ''Of course we have to protect sources and methods,'' Ms. Harman said in an interview Tuesday. ''But the point of requesting this report was to tell the public what happened.''

Sarah Little, a spokeswoman for Senator Pat Roberts, Republican of Kansas, the chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said he would not decide what might be declassified until he had read the report. Ms. Little said Mr. Roberts was traveling in his home state this week and would probably not see the report until next week.

The Mars rover Spirit has dug up more evidence of water on the red planet, scientists said yesterday.

At a news conference at the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., Dr. Steven W. Squyres, the mission's principal investigator and a professor of astronomy at Cornell University, said the rover found residue of sulfur and magnesium in a trench it had dug in the Gusev Crater in concentrations that suggest the minerals are combined as magnesium sulfate, or Epsom salt.

Finding the salt below the surface suggests that water percolated through the soil, Dr. Squyres said, dissolving the minerals and leaving a residue of salt. He called it ''much more compelling evidence than we have found anywhere else'' of water in the Gusev Crater region.

''We're not talking about big standing bodies of liquid water'' in the distant Martian past, Dr. Squyres said. ''You don't need a lake to do this. You can perfectly well do this with small amounts of water percolating through the soil,'' he said.

The other Mars rover, Opportunity, found evidence earlier this year of a great deal of long-ago water on the other side of Mars.

NASA scientists said yesterday that Opportunity was making a tentative foray into a large crater, Endurance, that has layers of stratified rock that promise to tell more of the story of Martian geological development. The rover will pull out after providing some scouting data, Dr. Squyres said, and will allow scientists to check the traction by examining the tread marks in the soil.

Dr. Squyres said that NASA tests on Earth suggested that the rover would be more than capable of climbing out. Even so, said Dr. Firouz Naderi, manager of the NASA Mars Exploration Program, ''the potential science benefits of sending Opportunity into the crater are well worth the calculated risk the rover might not be able to climb back out.''

Spirit is on its way to a formation known as the Columbia Hills, where scientists hope it will be able to examine bedrock-- whether on the hills themselves, or in chunks of rock that have tumbled from the heights.

''There is no textbook that tells you how to explore a mountain range with a robot,'' Dr. Squyres said.

Microsoft has hired Steven Berkowitz, the chief executive of Ask Jeeves, to run its floundering Internet division, Microsoft said yesterday.

Mr. Berkowitz became president of Ask Jeeves in 2001 and chief executive in 2003. He helped transform the service, which was introduced to answer questions posed in English phrases, into a search engine to compete with Google. Mr. Berkowitz continued to run the company after it was acquired by IAC/InterActiveCorp last July.

Microsoft has been struggling to redefine its online strategy and build an advertising-based business to confront competition from Google, Yahoo and others. The company's MSN service, which dates from 1994, has gone through a series of sharp strategy shifts as Microsoft has wrestled with whether it is a media company as well as a software vendor.

Most recently, the company decided to revive its effort to build advertising-based businesses as it sees Google give away free software, supported by advertising.

Despite a large investment to develop and promote its new search engine, Microsoft's share of the search market in the United States has plummeted. In March, it had 13 percent of the search market, down from 16 percent a year earlier, according to comScore Networks. Ask Jeeves held its share constant at 6 percent over the same period.

Microsoft's MSN Internet division over all was the second-most-visited network of sites in the United States, with 110 million visitors in February, unchanged from a year earlier, according to comScore. Yahoo, the No. 1 site, increased its audience 4 percent, to 120 million.

In an e-mail message to employees, Kevin Johnson, the head of the Microsoft division that includes Windows and Internet services, said Mr. Berkowitz would be a senior vice president, succeeding David Cole, who is going on leave in May.

Mr. Berkowitz, however, will have more limited responsibilities than Mr. Cole had. He will run marketing, sales and business development for MSN and the new Windows Live brand, which is meant to incorporate Microsoft's mail, instant message and search services. He will not oversee product development. His appointment was first reported on the Web site of The Wall Street Journal.

Development of e-mail and other communications services is run by Blake Irving, and search development by Steven Sinofsky.

An IAC/InterActiveCorp spokeswoman said that for now Mr. Berkowitz's responsibilities would be assumed by Doug Lebda, its president.

This autumn's recall of Firestone light truck tires led to the Ford Motor Company's first quarterly drop in operating income in four years and has prompted Bridgestone/Firestone to undertake a broad reorganization, with Japanese executives taking control of key operations, the companies announced today.

''It was a difficult quarter because of the Firestone incident,'' he said.

UNFAMILIAR bacteria have ruined many a vacation, turning intrepid travelers into tummy-aching wrecks.

Instead of trusting the water at their destinations, vacationers can zap bacteria with the Steri-Pen, a handheld machine that uses ultraviolet light to disinfect up to 16 ounces of water in about a minute. The pen emits UV-C rays, which prevent bacteria from reproducing by altering their DNA. ''It's not the microbes that make you sick,'' said the pen's inventor, Miles Maiden. ''It's when they reproduce and start having a party in your stomach.''

Mr. Maiden, 43, invented the product after 15 years as a solar power researcher and consultant. In 1996, while installing solar water-heating systems, he remembered that a narrow band of light rays, known as UV-C, had germicidal properties. Many bottling plants and municipalities use ultraviolet lamps to disinfect water, so Mr. Maiden had an idea: Why not install solar-powered water decontamination systems in third-world countries?

That idea proved too daunting, so Mr. Maiden, who has a degree in human ecology from the College of the Atlantic, miniaturized his idea to something more achievable: personal disinfection systems. In 1997, he founded Hydro-Photon in Blue Hill, Me., to develop the product. He whittled crude prototypes from wood.

''I wanted to gauge the public's interest before I spent a lot of time or money on the project,'' Mr. Maiden said, so a few months into his research, in 1998, he sent his idea to Newsweek magazine. When the magazine published a profile of the notion, he decided to proceed.

Hydro-Photon was formed to assemble and sell the pens. Mr. Maiden enlisted three different companies to create the pen's lamp, circuitry and plastic case. He began selling the Steri-Pen in 2001 (www.hydro-photon.com) for $199. It is also available in camping-goods catalogs.

Motorola Inc. and Palm Inc. plan to announce today that they will collaborate on a new portable phone that would put the features of a Palm hand-held computer into a device closer to the size and shape of a cell phone.

The companies said they had signed an agreement to use Motorola's wireless technologies, product line and distributors and Palm's core hand-held software technology. The effort is an extension of an agreement in December 1999 under which Motorola took a minority stake in Palm.

This deal, coming after a similar agreement last year between Palm and Nokia, could be a blow to Symbian, a consortium set up by Ericsson, Psion, Nokia and Matsushita Electric Industrial. Symbian has created a standard operating system, called EPOC, for wireless devices. In addition to Palm OS, the competition for Symbian also includes the Microsoft Windows CE operating system for mobile devices.

Mike Zafirovski, president of the Motorola PCS division, said the company had been working with its own operating system, as well as Palm and Symbian, and planned to continue all three efforts.

''Obviously a number of companies are working with various devices,'' he said. ''We're absolutely convinced that putting our two companies together will produce the right product for the first quarter of 2002.''

The Palm arrangement with Motorola differs from those it has with Nokia, Qualcomm and Kyocera, which are straight licensing agreements.

''What makes Motorola unique is it's jointly branded, and we're working closely together,'' said Alan Kessler, Palm's chief operating officer for products and platforms.

The first product of the collaboration is to be a G.S.M. wireless phone, expected to be available early in 2002, which will initially be distributed through the existing Motorola sales channels.  G.S.M. is the cell phone standard commonly in use in Europe and Asia, and the use of it is beginning to expand in the United States.

Combining technologies from both companies, the device will contain a larger color screen than standard mobile phones and will  include Palm's HotSync software and over-the-air synchronization using the Starfish TrueSync software from Motorola. Synchronization allows the hand-held device to keep up to date with information on the user's desktop computer. Mr. Zafirovski said the device would be larger than the smallest cell phones, but smaller than a typical Palm device.

Prices have not been set yet.

In Washington-speak, it is the P.D.B.  or President's Daily Brief. An intelligence digest prepared six mornings a week, by the Central Intelligence Agency, it is one of the most highly classified documents prepared by the government, its distribution limited under President Bush to fewer than a dozen senior administration officials.

Compiled in a loose-leaf notebook, and consisting of about a dozen items a day, the P.D.B. in some ways serves as a kind of newspaper, with reports on current developments around the world and on broader trends. On Aug. 6, 2001, the digest presented to Mr. Bush in Crawford, Tex., included a memorandum titled ''Bin Laden Determined to Attack Inside the U.S.'' Until Thursday, when it was publicly disclosed by Condoleezza Rice in her testimony before the special commission looking in the Sept. 11 attacks, even that title was classified.

As part of their continuing inquires into the Sept. 11 attacks and prewar intelligence about Iraq, both the Sept. 11 commission and the Senate Intelligence Committee have battled with the White House to gain access to the daily briefs. The White House has resisted, arguing that the documents are protected by the doctrine of executive privilege. So far, the White House has relented only to the commission, and only by allowing members of the panel to review a limited number of digests.

Whether Mr. Bush is in Washington or traveling -- or, as he was on Aug. 6, at his vacation home in Crawford -- the daily briefs are presented to him each Monday through Saturday by a C.I.A. official.

Asked on Thursday who had written the headline on the Aug. 6 report, a C.I.A. official declined to identify that person. A small unit of intelligence analysts within the C.I.A.'s Directorate of Intelligence prepares the daily brief, with input from other intelligence agencies.

Texas Instruments will announce today that it has integrated most of the computing functions of a mobile phone onto a single microchip, an innovation that may lead to lower manufacturing costs and improvements like longer battery life and higher data transfer rates.

The company plans to have the more integrated semiconductor widely available by the middle of 2006, making it the first major manufacturer to produce an integrated cellphone chip for the mass market, according to industry analysts.

At present, the components of a mobile phone include numerous specialized chips that control functions like sending and receiving radio frequencies, managing power and overseeing the phone's basic computing functions.

''This isn't an incremental step,'' said Bill Krenik, manager of wireless advanced architectures for Texas Instruments. ''It's a big leap forward.''

Texas Instruments is not the only company to have integrated much of that technology on a single chip. Last November, Qualcomm said it had developed integrated technology. However, its product may be in the mass market somewhat later than the Texas Instruments technology, said Alex Slawsby, an industry analyst with IDC, a research firm. Qualcomm said its chip would be available in the second half of 2006.

Mr. Slawsby said that the advantage of such chips might come initially in the production of inexpensive entry-level phones. The integrated chip, Mr. Slawsby said, would allow phone manufacturers to more quickly and cheaply produce handsets that could be sold to emerging markets.

Despite the advances toward integration of functions onto a single chip, some will remain separate. Specifically, the major chipmakers have not yet figured out how to economically integrate the memory, a specialized chip that stores phone numbers and other information.

A significant advancement is that the technology integrates two basic chips, Mr. Krenik said, the one that controls sending and receiving radio frequencies and the one that controls basic computing functions.

Saudi Arabia has sent its foreign minister to Washington to meet with President Bush on Tuesday, an administration official said tonight.

The foreign minister, Prince Saud al-Faisal, is expected to raise with Mr. Bush and other administration officials his country's concern about reports that classified sections of a Congressional study about the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, found that senior Saudi officials had funneled hundreds of millions of dollars to organizations that might have helped pay for them.

The foreign minister's hurriedly arranged visit reflects sensitivity in Saudi Arabia to the suggestions that, knowingly or unknowingly, it might have aided the terrorists who attacked the United States. Saudi officials have denounced any suggestions that they helped pay for the attacks.

The visit could also add to the pressure on the administration to declassify a 28-page section of the report, which was deleted from the nearly 900-page declassified version released Thursday by a joint committee of the House and Senate intelligence committees. People who saw the section have said it focuses on the role foreign governments played in the hijackings, but centers almost entirely on Saudi Arabia.

Senator Bob Graham, Democrat of Florida, a co-chairman of the investigation into the intelligence failures behind the attacks, called on the White House earlier today to make the classified section public.

Releasing it, said Mr. Graham, a candidate for his party's presidential nomination, would ''permit the Saudi government to deal with any questions which may be raised in the currently censored pages, and allow the American people to make their own judgment about who are our true friends and allies in the war on terrorism.''

The Saudis have made it clear that they intend to fight back against any assertion that they were involved in the attacks. Some Saudi officials have said the organization behind them, Al Qaeda, is as hostile to Saudi Arabia's rulers as it is to the United States, or nearly so.

After the Congressional report was released last week, the Saudi ambassador to the United States, Prince Bandar bin Sultan, called the accusation that his country had helped pay the terrorists ''outrageous'' and added, ''The idea that the Saudi government funded, organized or even knew about Sept. 11 is malicious and blatantly false.''

Several thousand protesters demanded an end to organized crime and corruption in government Saturday, as well as a reduction in the powers of President Kurmanbek Bakiyev.

The protest, the second in a month, comes amid rising dissatisfaction with Mr. Bakiyev, who took over last spring after a popular uprising overthrew his predecessor. Before assuming office, Mr. Bakiyev said he would reform the Constitution to limit the powers of the president, but has not done so.

The crowd of around 5,000 gathered in the main square of the capital near the presidential offices carrying banners with slogans like ''Constitutional Reforms Through Parliament'' and ''Yes to Democracy, Yes to Reforms!'' The protest was orderly, and a large number of police officers roamed the periphery of the march.

President Bakiyev has the power to dissolve Parliament, which he has threatened to do, and controls much of the country's media, both of which the protesters object to. But the group also wants to limit so-called family businesses, or enterprises linked to the first family.

Reports of nepotism under the former president, Askar Akayev, galvanized opposition to his rule and led to his ouster. Mr. Bakiyev is believed to have since taken over many of Mr. Akayev's assets.

The protesters read a list of demands, which included economic changes designed to address rampant unemployment and poverty in this remote, mountainous country.

''Today, we again give the authorities a deadline,'' said Kubatbek Baibolov, a lawmaker, setting a September target date for a new constitution. ''However, if this time they do not take real steps to meet these demands, we retain the right to insist on the tandem's resignation.''

Mr. Baibolov was referring to the uneasy power-sharing agreement between Mr. Bakiyev and Prime Minister Felix Kulov. It is unclear how supportive Mr. Kulov is of the opposition, but he has made public statements indicating that he agrees with many of its criticisms of the administration.

Politics in Kyrgyzstan is tumultuous. Five prominent political figures have been assassinated in Bishkek in the past year, four of whom were elected deputies to Parliament.

A reputed mafia kingpin, Rysbek Akmatbayev, was gunned down on May 10 -- a month after he was elected to Parliament. The government did not recognize his election, though, because of pending murder charges against him.

Mr. Akmatbayev, whose rise to power drew heavy criticism from the United States and Russia, was widely seen as the president's link to organized crime. Analysts say that his death has weakened the opposition by eliminating that perceived link and, with it, a major argument against President Bakiyev.

Trying to resolve a protracted tug of war between rival phone companies, a court-appointed arbitrator ruled yesterday that Gary D. Forsee can leave BellSouth to become chief executive of Sprint. But the arbitrator, William H. Webster, placed restrictions on what Mr. Forsee can do for the company.

Sprint has been trying for two months to hire Mr. Forsee, the vice chairman of BellSouth, to succeed William T. Esrey, whom Sprint's directors asked to step down amid a controversy about tax shelters. BellSouth, a local phone-service provider based in Atlanta, sued in state court in Georgia to enforce confidentiality and noncompete clauses in Mr. Forsee's contract.

Mr. Webster, a former federal judge who was director of central intelligence and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, sought to protect BellSouth's confidential information by prohibiting Mr. Forsee from participating in discussions about mergers and acquisitions or sales of assets at Sprint for 12 months.

Mr. Forsee, a former Sprint executive, will also be barred for a year from involvement in any efforts to recruit or hire BellSouth employees, or planning strategy for marketing combinations of wireless and land-line services or local and long-distance services in regions served by BellSouth. Sprint's directors will have to acknowledge publicly the restrictions imposed by Mr. Webster, BellSouth said in a statement.

Sprint said in a statement last night that the conditions set by Mr. Webster were acceptable and that Mr. Forsee would become chief executive and a board member today. A temporary restraining order that prevented Mr. Forsee from joining Sprint expired yesterday. The company added that Mr. Esrey would continue as chairman during a transition period.

''Gary is a proven leader and will do an excellent job heading Sprint,'' Mr. Esrey said in the statement. ''I am confident he will build on Sprint's strong foundation and further advance Sprint's position in the marketplace. We welcome him home.''

BellSouth said it had not given up the fight to prevent Mr. Forsee from joining Sprint, which is based in Overland Park, Kan. In its statement, BellSouth said that Mr. Webster had reviewed only the confidentiality clause of Mr. Forsee's contract. It said it would continue to seek favorable rulings from the Georgia Supreme Court on its other claims.

As Republicans gear up to try to reclaim control of the Senate next year, they view Senator Jean Carnahan of Missouri as one of the most vulnerable Democrats. They note that she did not win the seat in her own right, but was instead appointed to fill it after the death of her husband, Mel. The Republicans contend that she is a political novice who will not be able to fend off their more experienced candidate, former Representative Jim Talent.

Still, Republican strategists are worried.

As in many states, there is evidence in Missouri of a gender gap when it comes to how women vote, with many who live in the suburbs tilting Democratic. And no one is more aware of that tilt than Mr. Talent.

In an unsuccessful campaign for governor last year, he won 43 percent of the women's vote compared to 54 percent for his Democratic opponent, Bob Holden.

Now Mr. Talent finds himself not only facing a Democrat again, but a Democratic woman at that and, perhaps worse, a recently widowed Democratic woman. What is more, she is the sole woman the state has ever had in the Senate.

What to do?

Enter a new Missouri political group, Women for Talent.

It held its kickoff luncheon on Tuesday, in a St. Louis suburb, with almost 600 Republican women showing up, among them Catherine Hanaway, minority leader of the Missouri House. Ms. Hanaway told the gathering:

''They are going to tell you that you should vote for the other Senate candidate just because she has a set of ovaries. It is no more right to vote for a woman than it is to vote for a man, based on biology.''

Since then he has struggled to improve his standing with voters. But poll after poll has shown him lagging 10 points or so behind his popular Republican challenger, former Governor George Allen.

Until recently.

Now it appears Mr. Robb may be closing the gap. A poll published last week by The Richmond Times-Dispatch showed him trailing Mr. Allen by only three points, with about 10 percent of the electorate still undecided.

''Chuck always gives us heart failure in these elections,'' she told the crowd.

The most advanced spacecraft ever sent to Mars will soon enter the most critical phase of its mission: slowing down enough to go into orbit around the planet.

NASA officials said Friday that the two-ton robotic craft, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, was near the end of a 310-million-mile journey from Earth that began last Aug. 12 at Cape Canaveral, Fla.

The orbiter is to end its seven-month flight from Earth with a critical firing of its main engines on March 10 to slow the craft enough for the gravity of Mars to pull it into orbit. If something goes wrong with the 27-minute engine firing, the craft will zoom past the planet and go on into a useless orbit around the Sun.

''We're getting into the dangerous portion of the mission,'' James Graf, the project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California, said at a news conference at the agency's headquarters here.

''The cruise has not been easy,'' Mr. Graf said. ''We've accomplished an awful lot during that, but now we're starting to enter into the realm where we've lost two spacecraft in the last 15 years.''

The orbiter has to slow by 2,200 miles per hour, or about 18 percent, to go into an initial orbit with a high point of 30,000 miles and a low point of 250 miles.

Once locked around Mars, the craft will go through a seven-month period of dipping in and out of the atmosphere to drain off energy and slowly lower itself into a working orbit about 200 miles above the surface. Using this aerobraking technique saved more than 1,100 pounds of launching weight, allowing the spacecraft to be flown on a smaller rocket and saving millions of dollars, Mr. Graf said.

Slipping a spacecraft into Martian orbit is not easy, said Douglas McCuistion, head of NASA's Mars Exploration Program. NASA has only a 65 percent success rate in placing orbiters around Mars, he said at the news conference, compared with more than 80 percent in landing spacecraft on its surface.

''Mars is hard,'' he said. ''Mars can be unpredictable.''

Putting the newest Mars explorer into orbit will be hair-raising for its controllers, the officials said. About 21 minutes into the deceleration rocket firing, the craft will disappear behind Mars and remain out of contact for half an hour. After it re-emerges from the shadow of the planet, flight controllers will need 30 minutes to analyze its signals to determine whether it achieved orbit.

''This will be nail-biting time,'' Mr. Graf said.

The spacecraft's instruments will stay in hibernation during the months of aerobraking to reach its ideal orbit.

Iran's supreme leader said Tuesday at a meeting here with the Sudanese president that Iran was ready to share its nuclear technology with other countries.

''Iran's nuclear capability is one example of various scientific capabilities in the country,'' the leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, said to President Omar al-Bashir of Sudan, the news agency IRNA reported. ''The Islamic Republic of Iran is prepared to transfer the experience, knowledge and technology of its scientists.''

Mr. Khamenei made his comments just days before the Friday deadline set by the United Nations Security Council for Iran to suspend its uranium enrichment.

At a conference on Tuesday in Tehran on its nuclear program, senior officials vowed that Iran would continue its enrichment activities.

Iran's chief nuclear negotiator, Ali Larijani, said that in the event of Security Council sanctions, Iran would suspend cooperation with the United Nations nuclear agency. If there is a military strike aimed at destroying its facilities, Iran will simply hide its nuclear program, he added.

''You may inflict a loss on us, but you will lose also,'' he said.

Mr. Larijani said Iran was willing to cooperate if its case was returned to the International Atomic Energy Agency, but warned, ''Do not expect us to act otherwise if you drag the case to the Security Council.''

Ali Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, a senior cleric and head of the powerful Expediency Council, speaking at the conference, denounced the role of the nuclear agency and said it had failed to support Iran's program.

''I am not saying that the agency has had bad intentions,'' he said. ''But it has not fulfilled its duty to support countries to enjoy their right to have nuclear technology.''

It's a not-so-secret fact of political life that liberal interest groups sometimes make a point of endorsing Republican incumbents whose influence they need, even when Democratic challengers hold purer positions on the group's pet issues. That has caused bad feelings in some high-profile races this year.

In Oregon, the Human Rights Campaign, the national gay-rights group, has endorsed Senator Gordon H. Smith, the Republican incumbent, while Basic Rights Oregon, a state group with overlapping membership, favors the Democratic challenger, the state secretary of state, Bill Bradbury.

Roey Thorpe, executive director of Basic Rights, said the controversy had been painful. She acknowledged that Senator Smith had ''made a tremendous change in his approach to gay issues'' over the years, ''so I don't want to knock that at all.'' But she said that Mr. Bradbury had a stronger record in the state and that the choice had put some Human Rights Campaign members ''in a very awkward position.''

''They're supportive of the organization, and yet I doubt that they personally will be voting for Gordon Smith,'' she said.

David Smith, a spokesman for the Human Rights Campaign, said the situation ''certainly has been tense,'' but added, ''Senator Smith supports our major issues in Congress, and it is essential that we work with both parties because we cannot pass legislation without support from both and we cannot defeat hostile legislation without support from both.''

Hong Kong, a former British colony, was handed back to China in 1997 under a "one country, two systems" framework that guarantees the territory a high degree of autonomy and a separate legal system from mainland China. However, many Hong Kong residents feel that Beijing has been increasingly encroaching on their freedoms and autonomy in recent years.

The ruling has caused outrage among pro-democracy activists in Hong Kong, who argue that it is another attempt by Beijing to exert control over the territory. Some critics have suggested that the decision was made to ensure that the next chief executive is more closely aligned with the mainland government's policies and interests.

One prominent pro-democracy activist, Joshua Wong, expressed his concerns about the ruling on social media. "The decision to shorten the term of the next chief executive is a clear sign that Beijing is tightening its grip on Hong Kong," Wong wrote. "This is a blatant attempt to manipulate the political system and undermine the autonomy that we were promised."

The Hong Kong government has defended the decision, stating that it is in line with the territory's Basic Law and that it will ensure a smooth transition of power. However, many residents remain skeptical and worry that this ruling will set a precedent for further interference from Beijing in Hong Kong's affairs.

In response to the announcement, a coalition of pro-democracy groups in Hong Kong has called for a mass protest on Saturday to voice their opposition to the ruling. The protest is expected to attract thousands of participants and could potentially lead to further clashes between demonstrators and police.

The situation in Hong Kong remains tense, with many residents fearing that their unique political status is being eroded by an increasingly assertive Beijing. The ruling on the chief executive's term has only added to these concerns, and it remains to be seen how the people of Hong Kong will react to this latest development in their ongoing struggle for autonomy and democracy.

As the situation unfolds, the international community will be watching closely to see how Beijing's actions impact Hong Kong's political landscape and the future of the "one country, two systems" framework.

Emboldened by the strength of the pound and the euro, Europeans are eyeing real estate across the Atlantic, while the weak dollar is forcing Americans to think twice about property in Europe, analysts say.

William Thompson, vice president for sales at Newfound Property International in London, said luxury properties at the 200-unit Ocean's Edge Resort on the Caribbean island of St. Kitts, for example, are selling quickly, thanks in large part to Britons who are taking advantage of a favorable exchange rate.

''These buyers are taking a bet on the currency,'' he said. ''I can't predict where the dollar is going, but it seems to me to be a very nice time to buy if you can use pounds. And it could be very good for buyers if they use pounds to buy a dollar property and then the dollar strengthens.''

At Ocean's Edge, which is scheduled to be completed in January 2009, the one-bedroom beachfront apartments overlooking Cable Bay start at $315,000, or about 160,000 pounds. That is much less than the average price of a London property, which just hit 250,000 pounds, or about $490,000, for the first time.

''The Caribbean is definitely very attractive for Europeans right now, because it gives them the ability to buy dollar properties,'' Mr. Thompson said, adding that about 70 percent of the sales at Ocean's Edge had been to buyers based in Britain.

In recent months, the dollar has flirted with a 2-to-1 exchange with the pound for the first time since 1992. The dollar also recently hit a record low against the euro, with the European currency now worth about $1.31.

''Americans who are looking to diversify away from their home market will inevitably find the current circumstances surrounding the dollar more challenging,'' said Simon Rubinsohn, an investment strategist at Barclays Wealth in London.

''Rising interest rates in Europe also make the financing less compelling,'' he said. ''Our suspicion is that all this will continue to manifest itself in a lower level of interest in European property.''

There are no current, comprehensive sales figures on American real estate sales to foreigners or on American purchases in Europe, but industry experts on both sides of the ocean say there are substantial indications to support the flood of anecdotal evidence.

Richard Kirk, head dealer in charge of personal transfers at Travelex, the foreign exchange specialist in London, said his company had seen a 22 percent upturn this year in dollar trades from last year, when the pound was at $1.74. ''This is the weakest dollar we have seen for well over 10 years,'' he said, ''and it is no surprise that our clients are currently keen to transact.''

Mr. Kirk noted that a four-bedroom house in Florida on the market for $297,000 would be only 150,000 pounds, the price of a studio apartment in London.

Americans say that senators voting on Supreme Court nominees should consider the candidates' positions on issues like affirmative action and abortion before voting on whether they should be confirmed, according to the latest New York Times/CBS News Poll.

When asked whether President Bush's nominee for chief justice, Judge John G. Roberts Jr., should be confirmed, 63 percent said they were unable to offer an opinion. Of those who did, 26 percent said he should be confirmed and only 8 percent said the Senate should not vote to confirm him.

But Judge Roberts received more support from those who have been following the news about his nomination. Among respondents who said they were following news about Judge Roberts's nomination, 39 percent support his confirmation, and 11 percent said the Senate should vote against it.

Of all the respondents, most Republicans backed Judge Roberts; 51 percent said he should be confirmed and only 2 percent would rather see him rejected. Democrats were more closely divided: 13 percent for confirmation and 14 percent against. The rest did not offer a response.

In his two days of testimony before the Senate Judiciary Committee, Judge Roberts answered many questions from committee members but generally avoided providing his own legal views on issues like abortion and affirmative action, saying he did not want to be seen as prejudging any matters that might come before him if he joins the court.

Asked whether it was important that senators ''know his position on issues such as abortion and affirmative action'' before voting on Judge Roberts's confirmation, 46 percent said it was ''very important,'' and 31 percent said it was ''somewhat important.'' About 9 percent said it was ''not very important'' while 13 percent said it was not at all important, with the rest having no opinion.

The nationwide telephone poll was conducted Friday through Tuesday with 1,167 adults and had a margin of sampling error of plus or minus three percentage points.

Proving that he retains his theatrical flair, Col. Muammar el-Qaddafi, the Libyan leader, takes credit for President Bush's re-election in an interview to be broadcast Friday on Italian television.

In what is being billed as Colonel Qaddafi's first televised interview since United Nations sanctions were lifted last year, the iconoclastic head of North Africa's richest nation delivered a characteristic performance, swinging between the serious and the absurd.

He told Giovanni Minoli of Italian state television's investigative news program ''We Are History'' that he was still waiting for the United States to reward him for giving up prohibited weapons.

He said the move was responsible for Mr. Bush's election victory and said he now wanted the United States and other Western nations to provide Libya with nuclear technology for nonmilitary purposes. He said Iran and North Korea might follow his lead if they saw that Libya was compensated for its actions.

''It was Mr. Bush who promised to reward Libya if we got rid of this program,'' Colonel Qaddafi said, according to an English-language transcript. ''We know that with this withdrawal, we contributed by 50 percent to his electoral campaign.''

He said Libya was now a partner in the American-led campaign against terrorism, adding that one of his country's greatest contributions in the fight was to ''present itself as a model of moderate Islam.''

''Theocratic regimes that base their political regimes on a reactionary, Salafite religious idea, will always be a base for terrorism,'' he said, in what appeared to be a veiled criticism of Saudi Arabia. .

He warned Europe against letting Turkey into the European Union, suggesting that its entry would lead to Islam's domination of Europe.

''The Islamic world, even the Islamic extremists, even bin Laden, rejoice for the entrance of Turkey in the European Union,'' he said. ''This is their Trojan horse.''

Colonel Qaddafi elaborated on his solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, calling for the creation of a single state called ''Isratine.''

''This narrow area between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea cannot possibly be enough for two states,'' he said, arguing that Israel, alone, will not survive with a fast-growing Palestinian population beside it. ''The solution is the foundation of one, single democratic state.''

On matters closer to home, he said he planned to invite ''all interested countries'' to discuss the stream of illegal immigrants from Africa to Europe. He did not say when.

Colonel Qaddafi also held to the conceit that he did not play an official role in governing the country.

''The power is now in the hands of the Libyan people,'' he said. ''Every Libyan, man or woman, exercises the power, every Libyan over 18 of age, man or woman -- they all participate in the popular congress and in the people's committees. I do not exercise any power.''
