BellSouth said yesterday that it had not shared customer calling records with the National Security Agency, denying a report last week that it was among three major telephone companies to have done so.

BellSouth, the country's third-largest local phone company, said that after an internal review it had found no evidence that it had even been contacted by the agency.

''From the review we conducted, we cannot establish any link between BellSouth and the N.S.A.,'' Jeff Battcher, the company's spokesman, said in an interview. ''We wouldn't have made this bold statement if we weren't confident about this.''

USA Today reported on Thursday that BellSouth, along with AT&T and Verizon, had handed over their customer calling records without warrants as part of the security agency's efforts to build a huge database for use in tracking terrorists. AT&T and Verizon yesterday reiterated statements that they were vigilant about privacy but would not comment on national security matters.

The USA Today report said Qwest was alone among the four Bell companies in turning down government requests for calling records. The company has declined to confirm or deny that account, though a former chief executive of Qwest has affirmed that he rebuffed such requests.

Representatives of USA Today did not respond yesterday to requests for comment on the BellSouth statement.

The paper's report last week prompted lawmakers to threaten to subpoena phone company executives. They also called on the Bush administration to explain how it had been using the phone records.

Yesterday, Representative Edward J. Markey of Massachusetts, the ranking Democrat on the House subcommittee on telecommunications and the Internet, asked the Federal Communications Commission to examine whether AT&T, Verizon and BellSouth had violated privacy safeguards under communications law.

The Lockheed Martin Corporation said last night that it would buy the Titan Corporation for $1.8 billion in cash and stock to handle more of the government's communications systems and information networks.

''We are expanding our footprint in our traditional market, with the Department of Defense and federal civil agencies,'' said Jeffrey MacLauchlan, a Lockheed vice president for financial strategies and the head of its mergers and acquisitions unit.

Under the agreement, Titan's stockholders can choose to receive about $22 a share, a 30 percent premium over yesterday's closing price of $16.96. Titan shareholders may also opt for an equivalent amount of Lockheed Martin common stock or a combination of cash and stock. The transaction would include $580 million of Titan's debt.

The boards of both companies have approved the deal, which is expected to close in the first quarter of 2004. It is contingent on approval from Titan shareholders, the Justice Department and the Pentagon.

If approved, the acquisition would be Lockheed Martin's latest in a string of deals intended to increase its share of the government's business. Last month, Lockheed said it would acquire the federal information technology unit of Affiliated Computer Services.

''The other acquisitions were similar in that they were government-focused and they were information-technology focused,'' Mr. MacLauchlan said.

Titan, based in San Diego, does nearly all its business with the government, providing communications systems and products to gather intelligence.

Lockheed, based in Bethesda, Md., said it had no plans to move Titan or to close any of its operations.

FORGET for a moment the four C's: carat, clarity, color and cut. To the untrained eye, a diamond's beauty is most often judged by its brilliance.

''When you buy a diamond, you want people to notice that, wow, it's sparkling,'' said Randall Wagner, the president and chief executive of GemEx Systems in Mequon, Wis., who with his partner, Kurt Schoeckert, the company's vice president, developed a machine to rate this previously unmeasurable attribute.

Scientifically speaking, the machine, a BrillianceScope Analyzer, is an imaging spectrophotometer that scans stones. The analyzer shoots light through a diamond from five angles and measures how much of that light is returned to the eye.

In less than a minute, the analyzer produces a document with bar graphs to rate the diamond's brilliance against others. Since its introduction in 1998, the analyzer has measured more than 50,000 diamonds. A scale rates stones in three categories: return of white light, or brilliance; return of colored light, or fire; and scintillation, or twinkle. Because the cut of a diamond -- solitaire, emerald, marquise -- influences the amount of light reflected in it, the ratings compare diamonds only with others of the same cut.

Last year, GemEx began selling its light-analysis reports to retailers, wholesalers and diamond manufacturers. Retailers, including the Sterling Group and Zale's, for example, buy the reports at $30 to $40 apiece, depending on the stone's carat weight. More light translates into an increase in retail value, sometimes by almost 40 percent, Mr. Wagner said.

''We are not really grading the diamond for which is better,'' he said. ''Color and clarity define how rare the material is.'' And don't forget the size.

The Coast Guard is searching for a computer scientist from Microsoft who left for a daylong sailing trip off the coast of San Francisco on Sunday and did not return.

The man, James Gray, 63, who works in Microsoft's Silicon Valley research lab, set out alone Sunday morning for the Farallon Islands on his 40-foot boat, Tenacious, and was expected back that afternoon, Lt. Amy Marrs, a Coast Guard spokeswoman, said Monday.

Mr. Gray's wife notified authorities at 8:35 p.m. Sunday after he failed to return and did not answer cellphone calls, the Coast Guard said.

The Farallon Islands are about 25 miles west of the Golden Gate Bridge, and in optimal conditions the trip there and back takes about 10 hours.

Mr. Gray, who has worked at Microsoft for 10 years, researches databases and transaction processing systems. He is an authority on computer caching systems, which are meant to speed the transfer of frequently needed data or instructions. He received several computer science awards, including the prestigious Turing Award in 1998.

Before joining the research division at Microsoft, Mr. Gray worked at I.B.M. and at the Digital Equipment Corporation. His focus is on ''using computers to make scientists more productive,'' according to his Web site.

He has a longstanding interest in building supercomputers using inexpensive components to reduce the cost of storage. And he has been working with astronomers to build a powerful computer-based telescope.

''Our thoughts are with Jim and his family as we hope for his safe return,'' said Doug Free, a Microsoft spokesman.

Lieutenant Marrs said that Mr. Gray had more than 10 years of sailing experience and that his boat was well-equipped with communication, safety and emergency gear.

The San Francisco Bay Area has experienced good weather since Sunday morning. But local sailors consider this a particularly tricky time of year to sail to the Farallons, as distant storms can cause large swells in the shallow waters between the Golden Gate and the islands.

''This isn't just about Web sites anymore, and it's not about online shopping,'' said Ken Silva, VeriSign's chief security officer. ''It's about the way humans communicate and the way everything is interconnected.''

The potential challenge was underscored on Tuesday when an automated attack against the domain name system was carried out for several hours by a distributed computer program known as a botnet.

The attack initially affected all of the 13 root server systems -- the top level of the hierarchy of interconnected computers -- and then focused for several hours on servers operated by the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, the organization responsible for the Internet address system, and the Pentagon.

The attack impeded but did not halt any of the systems, according to several of the operators.

Such attacks make expansion of the name server systems crucial, Mr. Silva said. The VeriSign project, to be completed by 2010, will offer a tenfold increase in the capacity of two root servers that the company operates and of the infrastructure that supports the .com and .net systems.

VeriSign servers, now in 20 regional centers around the world, will be expanded to 70 sites. The effort would not only improve response time, the company said, but would also make it possible to diagnose and contain Internet attacks more quickly.

VeriSign profits indirectly from the growth of Internet traffic from its business managing the .com and .net domains.

In addition to resisting cyber attacks, the enhancement of the root server system is made necessary by the rapid growth in new types of Internet devices, many of which can communicate among themselves without direct human intervention.

The company said it expected the number of Internet users to grow from one billion today to 1.8 billion in 2010. Many will reach the Internet with multiple devices, including cellphones, most of which are expected to be Internet-enabled.

Less than two months after voters narrowly rejected an initiative that would have given Switzerland the most restrictive asylum laws in Europe, the Swiss government has signed an agreement aimed at curbing frivolous applications for political asylum.

The agreement with Senegal, signed last week in Dakar, Senegal's capital, allows Switzerland to deport to Senegal any West African whose asylum application has been rejected and whose country of origin is not clear.

Nearly all the 3,402 refugees from West Africa who arrived here in 2002 -- more than twice the 1,627 who came in 2000 -- have been denied political asylum, but fewer than 1 percent are thought to have given the authorities their true identities.

The Swiss say the agreement is a first step in combatting human traffickers operating in West Africa, by signaling that those with no legitimate reason for claiming asylum will not be allowed to stay.

Switzerland, with a population of 7.3 million, has the largest number of asylum seekers, per capita, in the developed world, according to United Nations statistics, and the number is rising. Switzerland provides refugees with housing, food and schooling for their children, a policy that emerged as a major issue in national elections in October. Last year, the government spent nearly $700 million to care for the 93,741 people who have been granted asylum or whose applications are pending.

Under the Senegal agreement, Swiss officials will accompany the rejected asylum seekers to Dakar and, working with African embassies there, try to identify their country of origin. If an identity cannot be established within 72 hours, the applicants will be sent back to Switzerland.

Swiss officials are expecting a sharp rise in asylum seekers with the European Union's introduction this month of a fingerprint data bank to enforce a unified asylum policy. Refugees rejected for asylum in one member country will not be permitted to apply in another. Switzerland, which is not a member of the European Union, would be one of the few alternatives for refugees.

Prime Minister Ariel Sharon won legislative approval for the government's emergency economic package on Wednesday, but emerged with a shrunken coalition after his dismissal of ministers from a strictly Orthodox party took effect early today.

It remained unclear whether the changed political map would lead to a reshaped coalition with new partners, or perhaps to early elections.

Mr. Sharon fired ministers from the strictly Orthodox Sephardic party Shas and deputy ministers from a smaller Orthodox party, United Torah Judaism, on Monday after they voted against the economic plan, which was narrowly defeated in Parliament.

Submitted again to the legislature on Wednesday, the budget-cutting plan was overwhelmingly approved, with most lawmakers from the two strictly Orthodox parties absent and some still voting against.

With the dismissals of the Shas ministers in effect today and both parties outside Mr. Sharon's coalition, his support in Parliament has been reduced to 60 seats from 82, making his government vulnerable to a no-confidence vote, which would force early elections.

Despite those risks, Mr. Sharon stood firm against any compromise with Shas, which had been an important member of his coalition with 17 seats in Parliament. He reportedly rebuffed a last-minute overture from Rabbi Ovadia Yosef, the spiritual leader of Shas.

However Mr. Sharon made no immediate moves to appoint replacements for the fired ministers, leaving open the possibility that they might negotiate a way back into his coalition after final passage of the economic package. The plan has to pass two more votes to become law.

Shas and United Torah Judaism opposed the plan, which includes cuts in government subsidies and welfare payments, because many of their supporters are from low-income groups, particularly full-time yeshiva students with large families who receive state assistance.

The $2.7 billion emergency plan was drafted to meet a budget deficit caused by an increase in defense spending to fight the Palestinian uprising, particularly the recent military offensive in the West Bank.

Although Mr. Sharon's parliamentary base is shakier now, his tough response to the rebellious ministers from Shas has won him wide public support. Although he is more heavily dependent on the Labor Party, his rival and partner in government, to preserve the coalition, he has the option of inviting other parties to join his cabinet, which would widen his base of support.

General Electric and Hitachi will merge their nuclear power businesses, the companies said on Monday, to provide services to owners of old reactors and to build new ones.

The announcement is another sign of global retrenchment in the field.

G.E. is competing to sell new reactors in the United States against Westinghouse, which is owned by Toshiba, and Areva, a French-German consortium. But with a 30-year gap in nuclear orders in this country, all three companies have limited experience in construction of the models they want to sell here.

John Krenicki, the president and chief executive of GE Energy, who spoke at the GE Research Center here, said of his new partner, Hitachi: ''They're currently building many new plants, and we see that as a major asset, being able to tap into that experience base.''

Akira Maru, chief executive of Hitachi Power Systems, said the company had one plant under construction in Japan and two in licensing. It has been in the nuclear business for more than 50 years, he said.

There are 95 reactors around the world that use the boiling-water design, the kind that G.E. builds, and Hitachi has been involved in 63 of them, Hitachi said.

The G.E. design boils water directly in the reactor vessel and uses it to spin a turbine, creating mechanical energy that is used to make electricity. Models marketed by other companies heat water in the reactor but keep it under pressure so it does not boil; that water is run through a heat exchanger to make steam. Advocates of the boiling water design say it gets more work out of the uranium fuel, and requires less steel and concrete.

Hitachi will take a 40 percent share of G.E.'s existing nuclear business, and G.E. will take about 20 percent of Hitachi's existing nuclear business, the companies said. The deal is supposed to close in the first half of next year. G.E.'s fuel business is not part of the arrangement.

General Electric's main design, the ''economic simplified boiling water reactor,'' has no orders yet but three companies are seriously considering ordering it. They are Dominion, for its North Anna site in Virginia; Entergy, for River Bend in Louisiana; and NuStart, a consortium established to build reactors, for Grand Gulf in Mississippi.

Two companies are considering building another G.E. model, the advanced boiling water reactor.

In today's fast-paced world, exercise has become an essential part of a healthy lifestyle. However, keeping track of one's physical activity can prove to be a difficult task, even for the well-intentioned. Devices like pedometers, which are commonly used to monitor physical activity, often provide only a crude measurement of one's exercise. Furthermore, they are not something most people would wear all day.

To better understand this issue, it is important to realize the limitations of traditional pedometers. These devices simply count the number of steps taken by the user, providing a rough estimate of the distance traveled. However, they do not account for differences in stride length or the intensity of the activity. This can lead to an inaccurate representation of one's exercise regime.

Moreover, pedometers are typically not designed for continuous wear throughout the day. Many people find them uncomfortable or impractical to wear during work or other daily activities. This can result in users forgetting to wear their pedometer or simply choosing not to use it, making it difficult to keep track of their exercise.

In response to these challenges, companies have developed more advanced devices, such as fitness trackers and smartwatches, which offer a more comprehensive and accurate measurement of physical activity. These devices not only count steps but also track heart rate, calories burned, and even sleep patterns. Additionally, they are designed to be worn all day, making them a more convenient option for those looking to monitor their exercise.

Despite these advancements, some users still struggle with maintaining consistent use of these devices. Factors such as cost, technical difficulties, or simply forgetting to wear the device can hinder their effectiveness in tracking exercise. It is important for individuals to find a method of monitoring their physical activity that best suits their needs and preferences.

In conclusion, while keeping track of exercise can be a difficult task, advancements in technology have provided more accurate and user-friendly options. It is essential for individuals to find a device that works for them, in order to maintain a healthy lifestyle and achieve their fitness goals.

IF you use a laptop computer while traveling, other people may be looking over your shoulder. But eShades, which look like a pair of oversized sunglasses, let you switch off the laptop monitor and view sensitive material privately. And to the outside world, you might just look like Joe Cool.

When plugged into a laptop, eShades offer a large-screen viewing experience: the images look as if they are on a 19-inch monitor two and a half feet away.

Alfred Hildebrand, the chairman of the eShades maker, Inviso Inc., a privately held company in Sunnyvale, Calif., has founded or worked with several companies involved in laser or optical technology. He was a co-founder of InViso in 1994, when he was a venture capital investor.

To combine the benefits of the fax machine and his pager's portability, Mr. Hildebrand developed small screens to allow a pager to receive a fax message. As portable communications devices proliferated, he then redesigned the displays for personal digital assistants and laptop computers. Mr. Hildebrand produced a final eShades prototype in May 2000. The glasses will be sold starting early next year.

The displays in eShades work much like traditional laptop displays. Liquid crystal is sandwiched between two pieces of glass, and a silicon chip imbedded in the glass transmits electronic signals that cue the crystal to create the desktop image. The flat-panel liquid crystal display is about an inch from each eye; an optical magnifier creates the feeling of a large display. ''It's like looking at a big-screen TV,'' Mr. Hildebrand said. Because the lighted image is so small, the battery uses only about a quarter of the power of conventional laptop displays.

EShades, which weigh about twice as much as regular sunglasses, will cost about $500, but Mr. Hildebrand expects the price to drop to about $300 ''sometime later on,'' he said.

Prudential Financial, one of the biggest life insurers, said last night that it had agreed to buy the retirement investment business of Cigna, a leader in health insurance, for $2.1 billion.

The deal will push Prudential into the top ranks of companies that operate 401(k) plans for employers and traditional pension plans for labor unions and universities and enable Cigna to focus more attention on health insurance, which has been providing 70 percent of its revenue.

Arthur F. Ryan, the chief executive of Prudential, has been buying and selling businesses to concentrate his company's efforts on life insurance and investments.

He said last night that the Cigna retirement units were ''an excellent fit that will strengthen the business we want to grow.''

H. Edward Hanway, the chief executive of Cigna, said his company would use the proceeds of the sale to pay off debt, strengthen its health insurance business and perhaps repurchase stock, which often provides a lift to share prices.

Cigna reported a loss of $398 million last year, mainly because of heavy claims against insurance it had sold to other insurers related to variable annuities, a form of mutual fund that includes life insurance. Its pension and health insurance businesses remained profitable, said Wendell Potter, a company spokesman, but profits in health insurance declined.

The company has exited the business related to variable annuities, he said, and on Oct. 31 reported third-quarter earnings of $195 million compared with a loss of $877 million in the period a year earlier. Before the sale of the pension units, Cigna was projecting profits of at least $755 million for 2003. Earnings will be lower because of the sale, Mr. Potter said, ''but we still expect a sizable profit.''

The purchase of the Cigna business will double the number of people with 401(k) plans run by Prudential, to 2.2 million, and add 700,000 people with traditional pension plans, raising Prudential's total to 1.3 million people.

The New Orleans city charter limits mayors to two terms. But Mayor Marc Morial, nearing the end of his second term, wants to serve three. He says there is still work to be done.

Mr. Morial argues that beyond the quaint charm and jazzy fun of the city's world-renowned French quarter, major economic and social problems remain, the most serious being a steadily deteriorating school system. So last week he proposed changing the city charter -- on a one-time basis -- so that he could take care of unfinished business. After that, he said, the two-terms-only limit would automatically be reinstated.

Changing the charter would require a referendum. The city council could call a special election and put one on the ballot, but its members (several of them possible mayoral candidates) oppose any change. So do three of every five voters, according to one poll.

Besides, some council members argue, the city's schools are run by an independent school board, not the mayor, though some legislators and community leaders favor changing that.

Mr. Morial, whose poll numbers have been good throughout most of his two terms, insists he will not be deterred.

''We shouldn't be afraid to say it,'' he said. ''The schools are in crisis. It's the defining battle of the early part of the 21st century in this city. Everyone should welcome help. The issue is bigger than any person, personality, entity, enterprise or interest group.''

Because the city council refuses to call a referendum, the mayor went on, he plans to put the issue on the next election ballot by gathering 10,000 petition signatures. And if necessary, he warned, he will spend $1 million to see that it passes.

''I want to lead this effort,'' he said. ''I've never started a race and not finished it.''

This has frustrated some on the left who feel that these groups are sacrificing their principles for short-term gains.

By working with politicians from both parties, they can advance their goals even when their preferred candidates are not in power. This is especially important in cases where Republicans hold significant influence or control over key committees or legislative bodies.

Despite the tensions that can arise from these endorsements, many liberal groups see them as a necessary part of their advocacy work. They believe that it's more effective to work within the existing political system than to hold out for ideal candidates who may never materialize.

Ultimately, the decision to endorse a Republican incumbent is a complex one that depends on a variety of factors. While some may see it as a betrayal of liberal values, others view it as a strategic move to achieve real-world results.

With less than six weeks to go until California's March 5 primary, the news just keeps getting worse for Representative Gary A. Condit.

Last week, three more top Democrats announced that they would not support his re-election effort in the state's 18th Congressional District in the upper Central Valley. All three -- Tony Coelho, who held the seat before Mr. Condit, and Dianne Feinstein and Barbara Boxer, the state's two United States senators -- said the fallout from the mysterious disappearance of Chandra Levy, the Capitol Hill intern with whom Mr. Condit reportedly had an affair, had ruined his chances of winning a seventh term.

''Time to move on,'' Mr. Coelho said.

''Time for a change,'' Ms. Feinstein said.

''Time for a fresh start,'' Ms. Boxer said.

Then all three called on Democrats to nominate Assemblyman Dennis Cardoza on March 5, saying that of the dozen or so hopefuls competing in the primary, Mr. Cardoza, who was once on Mr. Condit's staff, was best positioned to keep the 18th District out of Republican hands.

Mr. Condit scoffed at this latest demand that he pull out of the race, declaring, ''Not going to walk away.''

He has insisted from the start of the investigation of Ms. Levy's disappearance -- an investigation that continues -- that he has no idea what happened to her. The police say that while he has not always been as responsive to their questions as they would have liked, he is nevertheless not a suspect. Still, his poll numbers continue to slump, he is struggling to raise campaign cash and old allies continue to abandon him.

China said over the weekend that the last of four big state-owned banks would be financially restructured to prepare it for a public stock listing.

Three of the largest banks sold shares in 2005 and 2006, offerings that raised more than $40 billion and were among the most successful initial public stock issues anywhere.

The fourth financial institution, the Agricultural Bank of China, which has more than $500 billion in assets and upward of 500,000 employees, could go public as soon as next year, some analysts said.

The bank, which is closely tied to the country's struggling rural economy, was once dismissed as a candidate for public listing because it was China's most troubled bank. It has had the largest percentage of problem loans, or loans that are not producing income, and a record of fraud and mismanagement.

But at a high-level financial working group conference in Beijing, Prime Minister Wen Jiabao announced on Saturday that the Agricultural Bank's overhaul and listing would be pushed forward.

The decision, reported by state-run news media, did not come as a complete surprise. Many analysts had predicted that the Beijing authorities would press for the revamping and public listing of the bank, amid calls by foreign investors for stakes in China's banking industry.

In the last two years, some of the world's largest financial institutions -- including Citigroup, UBS, HSBC, Goldman Sachs and Merrill Lynch -- have invested billions of dollars to acquire minority stakes in big Chinese state-controlled banks ahead of public listings.

For many of those investors, the value of their investments soared after the three other state-owned banks went public in Hong Kong and Shanghai in 2005 and 2006. In October, for instance, the largest of them, the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, raised about $21.6 billion in what was the largest initial public offering in history. The two others to sell shares were the China Construction Bank and the Bank of China.

The feverish demand for Chinese banking stocks comes despite the mismanagement, corruption and poor lending practices. Some of the state-owned institutions were considered virtually insolvent five years ago, before the government began wiping debt off their books.

Investors are betting that China's efforts to revamp its big banks will bolster profits and allow the banks to benefit from the country's spectacular economic growth.

The government has spent five years and more than $400 billion purging bad loans from the books of the four leading state banks, helping prepare them to become shareholder corporations.

The Agricultural Bank is widely thought to be the toughest sell. The bank listed $93 billion in problem loans in 2005, or 26 percent of all loans.

Another challenge is that the bank, which is policy-driven, has put priority on the needs of China's 900 million farmers and other rural residents.

When it comes to diamonds, many people consider the four C's: carat, clarity, color, and cut. However, to the untrained eye, a diamond's beauty is most often judged by its brilliance. This refers to the way a diamond reflects and refracts light, creating a dazzling display of color and sparkle.

Brilliance is influenced by a diamond's cut, which determines how light is reflected within the stone. A well-cut diamond will reflect light back to the viewer's eye, creating maximum brilliance. A poorly cut diamond, on the other hand, may leak light from the bottom or sides, resulting in a lackluster appearance.

Color can also affect a diamond's brilliance. Diamonds that are colorless or near-colorless will reflect more light, while those with a yellow or brown tint may appear duller. However, some colored diamonds, such as pink or blue, can still be incredibly brilliant.

Clarity, or the absence of internal and external flaws, can also impact a diamond's brilliance. A flawless diamond will allow more light to pass through, resulting in increased brilliance.

Carat weight, while an important factor in determining a diamond's value, does not necessarily impact its brilliance. A smaller diamond with excellent cut, color, and clarity can still be incredibly brilliant.

Ultimately, a diamond's beauty is a subjective experience. While the four C's provide a baseline for evaluating a diamond's quality, it's important to remember that a diamond's brilliance is what truly captures the eye and heart. So, when shopping for a diamond, don't forget to take a moment to appreciate its dazzling brilliance.

The possibility of amending Russia's Constitution to allow President Vladimir V. Putin to extend his presidency beyond its legal end in 2008, now only a year away, has been a topic of debate for some time. Although President Putin himself has ruled it out, and the Kremlin was quick to do so again on Friday, the idea never quite dies.

In a recent press conference, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov reiterated the government's stance, stating that there are no plans to amend the constitution in order to extend Putin's term. "President Putin has made it clear on several occasions that he does not intend to change the constitution for his personal benefit," Peskov said. "We have a democratic system in place, and the president respects the will of the people."

Despite these statements, speculation continues to swirl around the possibility of such an amendment. Some political analysts and opposition figures argue that Putin's popularity and influence may make it difficult for him to step down from power when his term comes to an end. They point to the fact that Putin has been in power since 1999, first as prime minister and then as president, and that his approval ratings remain high.

One of the reasons behind this speculation is the lack of a clear successor for Putin. The Russian president has not groomed any obvious heir, leading to uncertainty about who might take over when he leaves office. This has fueled rumors that Putin may be considering a constitutional change to stay in power, despite his public denials.

Moreover, Russia's political landscape has shifted considerably since Putin first took office. The country has seen the rise of nationalist movements and a growing divide between the government and the opposition. Some argue that this environment may make it more likely for Putin to consider extending his term, as he may view himself as essential in maintaining stability and order in the country.

However, others contend that Putin's commitment to the rule of law and the democratic process will ensure that he steps down when his term ends. They point to his previous decision to step down as president in 2008, when he respected the constitutional limit of two consecutive terms and moved to the position of prime minister. In 2012, Putin returned to the presidency after his ally Dmitry Medvedev served a single term.

Some also argue that Putin may be more focused on securing his legacy and ensuring a smooth transition of power, rather than seeking to extend his time in office. They suggest that he may be working behind the scenes to identify a suitable successor who can continue his policies and maintain stability in the country.

In any case, the debate over the possibility of a constitutional amendment to extend Putin's presidency seems unlikely to subside anytime soon. As the clock ticks down to the end of his term in 2008, the speculation about Putin's future plans will only intensify.

Whether or not the constitution is amended, it is clear that Putin's influence on Russian politics will continue to be felt for years to come. His leadership has shaped the country in significant ways, and his departure from the presidency – whenever it may occur – is sure to have a profound impact on the nation's future.

Two weeks after returning to office after his brief ouster, President Hugo Chávez started to shake up his cabinet today by announcing the appointment of a new vice president and promising changes in the country's economic policy team.

Mr. Chávez's announcement that José Vicente Rangel, the defense minister, would replace Diosdado Cabello as vice president was not seen a major conciliatory move, since Mr. Rangel is considered a close associate of the president and vigorously defends his policies. But Mr. Rangel has a working relationship with business leaders, while Mr. Cabello is seen as an ideologue.

The president, who announced the changes on his weekly television and radio program, said he was going to ''make changes, and I'm starting with my economic team, revising economic policies.'' He added that more appointments would be made.

Mr. Chávez's opponents, as well as crucial allies in the National Assembly, have asked the president to replace ministers and to appoint officials more palatable to the business leaders who formed a coalition that carried out a series of antigovernment protests in recent months.

Those protests culminated on April 12 with Mr. Chávez's ouster when a peaceful demonstration degenerated into violence.

Mr. Chávez, who returned to power on April 14 with the help of loyal military officers, has promised to tone down his combative language and to rethink economic policies that had antagonized much of the country's middle and upper classes.

Although many opponents remain cautious about the president's pledge, Mr. Chávez has taken important steps since his return. He picked Alí Rodríguez Araque, the well-respected secretary general of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, as president of the state-owned oil firm and appointed a new board of directors, steps that were welcomed by company executives who had rebelled against a left-leaning board the president had appointed in February.

In the National Assembly, which is controlled by Mr. Chávez, leading congressmen have also said 17 of 49 controversial economic laws passed last year that caused considerable protest could be adjusted.

''We have no choice but to give Chávez the benefit of the doubt right now,'' one leading industrialist said today. ''The question that remains is whether he is willing to redefine his revolution or not,'' he added. ''We need to see actions, not words.''

Opposition politicians and businessmen have asked the government to replace Adina Bastidas, the minister of production and commerce, and Jorge Giordani, the minister of planning and a leader of the country's economic team. Both are considered ideologues whose policies have hurt the economy.

Mr. Chávez said Mr. Cabello would remain in the cabinet, but he did not specify in what position. He also did not say who would become the new defense minister.

The European Aeronautic Defense and Space Company, the parent of the aircraft maker Airbus, said on Monday that its board had unanimously approved a turnaround plan, one week after the Airbus chief executive had pleaded with its shareholders to overcome narrow national issues.

Details of the plan will not be released until meetings on Wednesday with Airbus workers' representatives from the four European countries where the company operates, EADS said.

The 10-member board voted to approve a revised version of an overhaul program, which is expected to result in the loss of thousands of jobs, mainly in France and Germany.

EADS expects the plan to eliminate around 5 billion euros, or $6.6 billion, in costs over the next three years.

The board abruptly suspended talks over the plan last week amid disagreements between French and German members over how the job losses would be distributed and where work on the company's next major aircraft project, the A350 XWB midsize jet, would take place. According to people with knowledge of the negotiations, the Airbus chief executive, Louis Gallois, presented a modified version of the reorganization plan to the EADS board on Monday.

The people with knowledge of the negotiations declined to provide further information, citing French labor laws that prohibit public disclosure of such details before labor representatives have been notified. Airbus is based in Toulouse, France.

Airbus warned last month that a two-year production delay in its flagship A380 superjumbo jet program and continued weakness of the dollar against the euro would result in a significant financial loss for 2006.

The aircraft maker has also warned that it may need to raise new money from shareholders to finance the A350 XWB, Airbus's competitor to Boeing's popular 787 Dreamliner.

Airbus has about 55,000 employees at 16 sites in Europe. This week, the French prime minister, Dominique de Villepin, said the overhaul plan would eliminate as many as 10,000 jobs -- roughly 18 percent of the work force -- a figure that EADS and Airbus executives have declined to confirm.

Analysts expect that many jobs will be eliminated through attrition, early retirements and termination of temporary work contracts. Further reductions will most likely come from the sale of several factories.

German newspapers reported last week that the original plan called for the sale of two industrial sites in the state of Lower Saxony. One plant, in Nordenham, builds fuselage shells and employs about 2,100. The other location, in Varel, has 1,100 workers and makes specialized aluminum and titanium parts. The French media have also cited union sources as saying some French factories in the north and west of the country could be sold.

Analysts have long argued that the plane maker should spin off the production sites that add the least value and focus instead on designing, assembling and testing planes.

The nation's leading semiconductor trade group said Wednesday that chip sales this year would set a record as the economy improves and demand for personal computers and cellphones continues to climb.

In its midyear report, the group, the Semiconductor Industry Association, projects that worldwide sales of semiconductors will grow to $214 billion this year, surpassing the $204 billion record set in 2000.

The group forecasts that worldwide chip sales this year will increase nearly 29 percent over 2003; last fall, it projected growth of 19 percent this year.

''The industry is experiencing substantially stronger-than-expected growth in 2004,'' said George M. Scalise, president of the association, which is based in San Jose, Calif. He said the chip industry was benefiting from growth in many areas, including personal computers, electronics, cellphones, telecommunications equipment and even automobiles. Strong demand for equipment used for wireless Internet connection is also contributing to growth in chip sales.

''The current cycle appears to be one of the more balanced cycles in the history of the industry, with growth coming from a very broad range of applications and in all geographic regions,'' Mr. Scalise said.

The association's report comes just a week after Intel narrowed its revenue forecast for the current quarter to the upper end of its earlier range, citing surprisingly strong sales of cellphones and other electronics products.

In more good news, capital spending for telecommunications is expected to grow 5 to 10 percent in 2004 -- the first increase since 2000, the association said.

John Greenagel, a spokesman for the association, said much of the growth in sales was coming from China, which makes up 15 percent of the chip market. Chip sales in the Asia-Pacific region have grown to 40 percent of the worldwide total.

Personal computer sales continue to account for the biggest portion of sales, representing roughly 30 percent of the chip market. They are expected to increase 13 percent in 2004, compared with the association's November 2003 forecast of 11 percent.

The growth is being driven not just by an increase in the number of devices sold but also by the rising number of chips used in digital electronics. Digital video recorders, for example, have four times the semiconductors of DVD players, and are selling at three times the rate of 2003. Similarly, the semiconductor content in cars is increasing about 10 percent a year.

Looking ahead, the industry association projects a compound annual growth rate of 10.4 percent from 2004 through 2007, though sales are expected to decline in 2006 and then rebound in 2007.

Some people may think that the art of building ornate pianos ended during the Depression. But Steinway & Sons, one of the nation's oldest piano makers, is out to prove them wrong. The company is planning a collection of recreations of famous pianos it built from 1850 to 1930.

Last week, at a Champagne-and-caviar reception in Midtown Manhattan, Steinway unveiled the first of them -- a $675,000 recreation of what is known as the Alma-Tadema piano, ''the grandest'' of the grand pianos, the company says.

Steinway plans to sell the pianos in the collection, each of which it says is one of a kind.

The brown-and-beige Alma-Tadema piano, named for its designer, Sir Lawrence Alma-Tadema, the British artist, contains 2,200 inlays of mother of pearl and makes ample use of brass, copper and bronze moldings. It also has nine laurel wreath moldings bearing the Greek names of the nine Muses and a molding that can be removed and replaced with a family crest. A copy of a painting by Sir Edward Poynter, ''The Wandering Minstrels,'' is embedded in the wood above the keyboard.

''Most people assume that the art of building art-class pianos is gone, that you can't do it anymore, that if you want something like that, you have to go to an antique shop,'' said Frank M. Mazurco, executive vice president of Steinway.

The original piano, built in 1887 for the Madison Avenue mansion of Henry G. Marquand, a millionaire art collector, was bought in 1997 for $1.2 million by the Sterling and Francine Clark Art Institute in Williamstown, Mass.

Aaron Donovan

Excelsior, the once prominent citadel of journalism that has been bought by a group of American and Canadian investors for $150 million, really died a quarter-century ago, when the rulers of the Institutional Revolutionary Party secretly bought its loyalty and over time drained it of independence.

It was born with the Mexican Revolution, in 1917, and was a formidable institution into the 1970's. But in 1976, President Luis Echeverría organized an internal coup at the workers' cooperative that ran the paper.

Politicians of the governing party bribed editors and reporters with money and other payoffs. The paper became an exemplar of a corrupt and decaying tradition of political advertising masquerading as news. Along with more than a few other Mexico City dailies, it would not have survived for long without the government money that propped it up.

Two years ago, when the election of President Vicente Fox ended the Institutional Revolutionary Party's control after seven decades, the under-the-table subsidies and payoffs had already ended. The newspaper announced that it was nearly bankrupt. Its debts totaled at least $75 million.

Today the paper's chief asset appears to be its office building in the center of Mexico City. Its members, who continued to own the paper cooperatively, threw out their director, Regino Díaz Redondo, and have labored to revive the paper, often without pay and almost entirely in vain.

The members did not disclose the buyers' identities, just their nationalities. They said they hoped that the sale would create ''an era of recuperation'' for Excelsior.

WPP Group, the large British advertising concern, is preparing to make a formal offer for the media-buying agency Tempus that values the company around £440 million, or $636 million, in an attempt to trump a previous offer from Havas Advertising of France, people close to the discussions said today.

WPP is expected to file its cash offer of £5.55 a share on Monday with British regulators, although it does not have the support of the Tempus board, a condition WPP initially insisted on, these people said. Instead, Tempus will withdraw its support for Havas's £425 million offer and remain neutral through what is expected to be a heated bidding contest.

A Havas spokesman, Simon Gillham, said, ''If there was another offer on the table, we would reconsider our position.''

Some analysts have suggested that Havas could raise its offer as high as £6 a share for Tempus, or 11 percent above its initial price of £5.41 a share in cash. But these analysts also say that WPP could outbid its rival because of a 22 percent stake in Tempus it has amassed over the last four years at an average price of £2 a share, lowering the overall cost of an acquisition.

Industry companies have been consolidating in an effort to piece together worldwide planning and buying agencies. Tempus is one of the few remaining independent operations, which is one reason it is attracting such attention. Another is Aegis, which analysts say could attract the attention of the company that does not succeed in winning Tempus.

With a strong foothold in Europe, Tempus's media-buying arm would complement the Media Edge, owned by WPP, which buys advertising space for clients primarily in the United States.

A formal offer from WPP is expected as the company reports half-year financial results on Monday, and it follows informal discussions between WPP and Tempus executives last week. The two camps met at the London offices of Lazard Frères, the investment bank advising Tempus, where Sir Martin Sorrell, WPP's chief executive, outlined a plan to create the fourth-largest media-buying company in the world with annual billings of $15 billion.

The Hubble Space Telescope has a new, resonant date with destiny. NASA has set Sept. 11, 2008, as the target date for launching a mission intended to revitalize the telescope and keep it spaceworthy into the next decade, according to a planning document made public by nasawatch.com, an independent Web site.

Three years ago, Sean O'Keefe, then the NASA administrator, decided to forgo Hubble telescope maintenance in the wake of the shuttle Columbia disaster, prompting a nationwide debate about the risks of shuttle flights and the value of the telescope. Michael D. Griffin, the current NASA administrator, reversed Mr. O'Keefe's decision.

In a series of spacewalks, astronauts from the shuttle Atlantis will replace vital gyroscopes and batteries and install a new camera and a new spectrograph, extending the telescope's capabilities into new realms of the electromagnetic spectrum, Dr. Griffin announced in October.

The selection of a noteworthy date, the seventh anniversary of the terrorist attacks on the United States, was not deliberate or official, said a spokesman for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration. The spokesman said that it was only a target date on an internal document and that it could change after a review. Shuttle schedules and launching dates are notoriously tentative, and delays often occur because of the complexity of the launching preparations.

This year, NASA plans five shuttle missions. But William W. Parsons, director of the Kennedy Space Center, said yesterday at a briefing that one of them could slip into next year.

TO alert them to incoming calls, owners of Nokia cell phones have a choice of more than a dozen tones and tunes, from Beethoven's Ninth Symphony (''Ode to Joy'') to ''Take Me Out to the Ball Game.'' But there is a signature melody, Francisco Tarrega's ''Gran Vals,'' written in the late 19th century, that unmistakably identifies the brand name.

Nokia started using it in advertising around 1994, when cellular phones were still relatively primitive. But Nokia's marketing man in Europe, Annsi Vanjoki, decided that the tune should be integrated into its phones -- partly to build the brand but also to signal to customers that they could hear something distinctive in a world where more and more mobile phones would be ringing simultaneously.

So he had the company's engineers reproduce the ring melody, as it is now called, in a very simple ''da-dee-da-dee-dum'' format and install it on phones as a default choice. The company did not have to pay royalties, because the copyright was long expired.

Mr. Vanjoki, 43, is now head of Nokia Mobile Phones for Europe and a member of the executive board of the Nokia Group.

Today, the tune is so ubiquitous on sidewalks and commuter trains and buses that Nokia executives worry that it may come across as annoying. Though available on most Nokia phones, it no longer is always the default ringing tone, and executives emphasize that the phones also offer many less intrusive alerts, like lights and vibrations. On the horizon are models that will let users log on to Web sites to compose and download their own ring melodies.

President Vladimir V. Putin has ruled it out, and the Kremlin was quick to do so again on Friday, but the idea never quite dies: amending Russia's Constitution to allow Mr. Putin to extend his presidency beyond its legal end in 2008, now only a year away.

The proposal seemed to gain new life when Sergei Mironov, the chairman of the upper house of Parliament, or Federation Council, proposed Friday not only to allow Mr. Putin to seek a third term but also to expand presidential terms to five or seven years from the current four.

''Four years is a short period of time for a large country like Russia,'' Mr. Mironov said in remarks delivered Friday after his re-election to a third five-year term.

Mr. Mironov is the leader of a new pro-Putin party, Just Russia, which critics have denounced as a Potemkin project to create the appearance of political competition in a system otherwise tightly controlled by the Kremlin. His proposal, which he claimed had the support of millions of Russians, certainly set off a debate -- mostly over who supported the president more.

Boris V. Gryzlov, the leader of the main pro-Putin party, United Russia, echoed Mr. Putin's previous statements that he opposed changing the Constitution, though the deputy speaker of the lower house, Lyubov Sliska, called it ''a good initiative,'' the Interfax news agency reported.

But there were harsh words as well. Gennadi A. Zyuganov, the leader of the Communist Party, suggested that the proposal was a misguided trial balloon. ''Today, the head of state has more powers than a pharaoh and a czar together,'' he said, adding that the president's authority should be the subject of debate, not presidential terms.

The Kremlin politely rebuffed the idea of altering presidential terms. But that did not deter Mr. Mironov, who has raised the issue before, though not with such a specific outline for adopting the necessary amendments to the Constitution.

''What Vladimir Putin has done in Russia and for Russians is a breakthrough,'' he said later in a television interview with Rossiya, the state television network, which devoted considerable coverage to the debate. ''A sense of pride has returned for Russians and, let's agree, only in the last two years we have lived in stability. Everything is only beginning.''

Lilia Shevtsova, a senior associate with the Carnegie Moscow Center, said the persistence of the idea underscored the uncertainty that pervades Mr. Putin's last year in office -- perhaps by design.

Although Mr. Putin has said he would express his support for a successor, and two aides have emerged as likely candidates -- Dmitri A. Medvedev and Sergei B. Ivanov, both first deputy prime ministers -- there is no consensus on who will take over and what the change could portend. That, she said, allows Mr. Putin to avoid becoming a lame duck.

NORMALLY, Viisage Technology of Littleton, Mass., catalogs drivers' licenses and other forms of identification for government offices. But nowadays, its technology, which converts video images, photographs or police composites of faces into strings of numbers, is being considered for airport security.

One product, FaceFinder, compares faces with those in a database, matching or discarding the image of the face in about one second. In recognizing criminals or suspects, said Tom Colatosti, chief executive of Viisage since 1999, FaceFinder ''automates what police officers do.''

The technology behind FaceFinder -- a series of equations based on 128 measurements of the face -- was developed by Alex Pentland, a professor at M.I.T. Viisage bought the rights in 1996. Since then, the company has refined the math and developed software for real-life identification.

In January, Super Bowl XXXV in Tampa, Fla., provided the first substantial test of the software. As 75,000 fans entered Raymond James Stadium, a Viisage-operated camera scanned faces, captured images and compared them with the faces of suspected criminals. If the camera did not capture a clear-enough image, a bell went off and the person had to pass by the camera again. ''It's like a metal detector at the airport,'' Mr. Colatosti said. Researchers at the Bell Laboratories of Lucent Technologies have created the first solid laser from organic materials that is electrically powered, a breakthrough that they and other researchers predict will lead to a wide range of new uses for laser light in communications and information storage.

The Bell Labs results, reported yesterday in the journal Science, were achieved with thin disks of a crystallized benzene-based material called tetracene. But the researchers said it should eventually be possible to manufacture such lasers in thin films that could be incorporated in plastic sheets, allowing them to be inexpensively produced in a wide variety of flexible shapes.

Such devices, which have been dubbed ''plastic lasers,'' are eventually likely to be cheaper than today's metal solid-state lasers. They are also likely to be more versatile, because organic substances can be relatively easily manipulated to emit light ranging from ultraviolet to infrared, according to Bertram Batlogg, the director of solid-state physics research for Bell Labs.

Most solid-state lasers are limited to the red and infrared portions of the spectrum. Lasers that emit light at the shorter wavelengths toward the ultraviolet end of the spectrum could lead to devices that transmit information more rapidly and store it more compactly. The lasers might also be used in medicine, chemical analysis and other areas where today's lasers are ineffective. .

Bell Labs' research also suggests that organic lasers might require far less energy than the metal semiconductor lasers used today in consumer and commercial devices and in telecommunications. The work reported in Science involved energy requirements comparable to those of today's solid-state lasers, but at a recent conference, Mr. Batlogg told researchers that lasing had been achieved with far lower energy inputs.

A wide variety of gases, liquids and solids can be pumped with energy under conditions that lead them to emit laser light, which consists of a beam or pulses that are all the same wavelength and in which all of the waves travel in synchronized peaks and troughs. Such ''coherent'' light is much more intense and focused than normal light.

Bell Labs' organic laser is a milestone that some doubted would ever be achieved. It was not until 1996, long after metal-based lasers were in wide use, that researchers were even able to confirm that it was possible for solid organic materials to be stimulated enough to emit laser light. But doing so required pumping huge amounts of energy from other lasers into the test materials, which tended to overheat and break down quickly.

For all the excitement, commercialization of the discovery is likely to take many years.

Executives who are longtime BlackBerry users will have to teach their right thumb some new tricks if they switch to a model introduced on Monday.

The model, the BlackBerry 8800, eliminates a tiny scroll wheel on the side that is intended to navigate through lists of e-mail messages. The plastic wheel has been a signature feature of all business-oriented BlackBerrys since the first model was released eight years ago.

In its place on the 8800 is a small front-mounted navigation ball developed for the BlackBerry Pearl, a consumer model released last year.

While the Pearl is an attempt by BlackBerry's maker, Research in Motion, to enter a larger and more competitive market, the 8800 is arguably a more important product. Priced at $300 in some plans from AT&T, the 8800 will be aimed at corporate and business users, a market segment dominated by Research in Motion, based in Waterloo, Ontario.

Mike Lazaridis, the president and a chief of R.I.M., said he anticipated that even hard-core BlackBerry users would find the ball easier to use, particularly when viewing Web pages and using some of the multimedia features introduced on the device, including a G.P.S.- based automatic mapping system.

The small, pealike ball, Mr. Lazaridis said, is as efficient as a computer mouse when it comes to navigating through screens that require movement from side-to-side rather than just scrolling up and down, the action needed for e-mail lists.

He also took an indirect shot at Apple's new iPhone, which uses a touch screen to achieve the same end.

''We're all used to having a mouse on our desk,'' Mr. Lazaridis said. ''But not many of us have a touch screen.''

Allen Nogee, an analyst at In-Stat, a market research firm, is far less skeptical about the iPhone's approach than is Mr. Lazaridis. But he added that the consumer reaction to the Pearl suggested that business users would not miss thumb wheels.

''Most people really take to it,'' he said. ''The wheel is problematic when you have to go two different directions.''

The 8800, which will first be offered by AT&T on Feb. 21, maintains the full keyboard that has always been featured on BlackBerrys intended for business and government users. Despite that, it is the thinnest hand-held ever offered by the company, a feature that Mr. Lazaridis said did not come at the expense of the battery's size.

The unit includes other features from the Pearl, like the ability to accept SD memory cards and play music as well as videos. Corporations can shut down or limit all of those features by remote control.

But Mr. Lazaridis said that corporate users concerned about security made it clear that they did not want a digital camera, which is not to be found on the 8800. ''There's a very strong demand out there for BlackBerrys without a camera,'' Mr. Lazaridis said. ''Not having one, that's a feature.''

The Chase Manhattan Corporation is negotiating to acquire the British asset management and investment banking firm Robert Fleming Holdings, the companies said today. A deal would end the independence of Fleming, one of Britain's last privately held banks.

Executives close to the talks said that an announcement of a purchase could come within a week, though the companies might still decide to abandon the effort. While a price for the British bank has yet to be fixed, the executives said, it is expected to exceed $:3 billion, or about $4.75 billion.

A purchase of Fleming would follow Chase's $1.35 billion acquisition of the Hambrecht & Quist Group last year, which helped strengthen Chase's high-technology investment banking business.

It would also give Chase, of New York, the third-largest American banking company, a powerful presence in Asia, where Fleming has a successful asset management practice, but not much more in Europe.

In a statement, Fleming said,  ''Discussions are at an early stage and no further announcement will be made unless and until appropriate.'' Unusually, Chase also confirmed the talks, but said it did so ''at the request of Robert Fleming Holdings.''

Analysts said a successful deal would still not give Chase the size to join the upper echelon of investment banks like the Goldman Sachs Group or Morgan Stanley Dean Witter.

''They are definitely getting a strong presence in Asia,'' said Tom Rayner, an analyst at SG Securities. ''But it's not going to help them compete much in Europe.''

Several analysts said a more logical purchase for Chase would be Dresdner Bank's Kleinwort Benson unit, which would give Chase an immediate investment banking presence in Europe at a time when mergers and acquisitions are occurring at a rapid pace. ''There are better propositions around,'' Mr. Rayner said.

Shares of Chase rose $6.9375 today, to $98.50. News of the talks was first reported in The Financial Times.

Fleming, which is not a publicly traded company, is 29.4 percent-owned by the Fleming family, which includes Ian Fleming, the writer who created James Bond. The company operates a joint venture with T. Rowe Price Associates, which has about $35 billion of managed assets. The bank also owns Jardine Fleming, which was once Hong Kong's biggest broker. In all, the bank manages $137.4 billion for its clients. Robert Fleming has about 7,800 employees with offices in more than 40 countries.

If Chase acquired Robert Fleming, the deal would bring a near-end to Britain's privately held banks. It would leave only Cazenove & Company as the last major British-based investment banking business.

Just last month, Citigroup bought the Schroders investment banking business for $2.21 billion.

Others sold to foreign companies in the last several years include Warburg Dillon Read and Barings.

The authorities in Beijing ordered on Wednesday that the next chief executive of Hong Kong serve only the remainder of the term of the previous chief executive, a ruling that critics of mainland policies toward the territory described as a further erosion of Hong Kong's autonomy.

The Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, China's Communist Party-controlled legislature, issued a legally binding interpretation of Hong Kong's Basic Law, its miniconstitution. The interpretation will limit the chief executive to be selected this summer to the two years remaining in the second term of Tung Chee-hwa, who resigned on March 12.

Stephen Lam, the secretary for constitutional affairs, told the legislature last spring that if Mr. Tung stepped down early, the Basic Law clearly called for the next chief executive to be elected for a full, five-year term. The Hong Kong Bar Association and other legal groups had reached similar conclusions, since the Basic Law made no mention of partial terms for chief executives.

But when Mr. Tung stepped down, citing stress but also after being publicly criticized by China's president, Hu Jintao, two mainland legal experts stepped forward to say they recalled discussing partial terms during the drafting of the Basic Law in the late 1980's. China's legal practice calls for consideration of the legislative intent of the drafters of laws, and the Hong Kong government ended up asking Beijing for an interpretive ruling.

The local government welcomed the ruling, saying in a statement that it ''removes the uncertainties affecting the normal operation of the government and the community, and ensures that the new chief executive will be elected smoothly and in time on July 10.''

Mr. Tung became chief executive with the transfer of Hong Kong to Chinese rule in 1997. Donald Tsang, the chief secretary, became acting chief executive when Mr. Tung resigned and he is the favorite to be selected for the two-year term when the city's Election Committee convenes July 10. Limiting the next term to two years will give Beijing more influence over Mr. Tsang, who was knighted for three decades of loyal service to the British and is distrusted by some pro-Beijing politicians.

The most advanced spacecraft ever sent to Mars is about to begin the most crucial phase of its mission: slowing down enough to enter orbit around the planet. The spacecraft, known as the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, has been traveling through space for over seven months and is now just a few weeks away from its destination.

The Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter was launched from Earth on August 12, 2005, and has been traveling through space at a speed of over 24,000 miles per hour. The spacecraft is equipped with a suite of scientific instruments that will allow it to study the Martian surface and atmosphere in unprecedented detail. These instruments include a high-resolution camera, a spectrometer, and a radar system that can penetrate beneath the surface of the planet.

The spacecraft will begin its critical slowing down phase on March 10, 2021. This phase will involve firing the spacecraft's engines to reduce its speed and allow it to be captured by Mars' gravity. The spacecraft will then enter an elliptical orbit around the planet, with a closest approach of just 250 miles from the surface.

Once the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter is in orbit, it will begin its primary mission of studying the Martian surface and atmosphere. The spacecraft will use its high-resolution camera to take detailed images of the planet's surface, which will help scientists better understand the geological history of Mars. The spectrometer will analyze the composition of the Martian atmosphere, looking for signs of water and other key elements that could indicate the presence of life.

The radar system on board the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter will also be used to study the planet's subsurface. By sending radar waves towards the planet and measuring their reflections, scientists will be able to create detailed maps of the Martian underground. This will help them better understand the planet's geology and the potential for future exploration.

The Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter is just one of several spacecraft currently in orbit around Mars. These spacecraft include NASA's Mars Odyssey and Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution (MAVEN) missions, as well as the European Space Agency's Mars Express mission. Together, these spacecraft are helping to build a detailed picture of the Martian environment and paving the way for future exploration.

The Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter is a testament to the ingenuity and expertise of the scientists and engineers who designed and built it. Its advanced scientific instruments and cutting-edge technology will allow us to learn more about Mars than ever before, and pave the way for future missions to this fascinating planet. As the spacecraft enters its critical slowing down phase, the world will be watching with bated breath, waiting to see if it can successfully enter orbit around one of the most intriguing planets in our solar system.

Since then, Barneys has been run by three of its executive vice presidents, who will now continue with their regular duties, the company said. Mr. Socol will succeed Mr. Questrom as chairman, but Mr. Questrom will stay on as a director.

The European Aeronautic Defense and Space Company named a new German co-chairman Thursday, tapping a longtime aerospace engineer who also played a central role in conceiving the group's delicate management structure.

The new executive, Rüdiger Grube, 55, had been widely expected to succeed Manfred Bischoff, who resigned Wednesday after being named chairman of DaimlerChrysler, one of EADS's core industrial shareholders.

Though he has been a member of the EADS board since 2004, Mr. Grube has kept a low public profile throughout a turbulent three years of boardroom power struggles and management fumbles that culminated in a major industrial crisis at Airbus, the group's largest division.

A spokesman for DaimlerChrysler declined to comment on Mr. Grube's role in the Chrysler talks.

Mr. Grube's first challenge over the next two weeks will be to resolve a dispute over a forthcoming capital increase, pitting the group's industrial shareholders against the French government, which owns an indirect 15 percent stake in EADS.

The French government is thought to prefer to raise the cash through a share sale, while both DaimlerChrysler and Lagardère are arguing in favor of a bond that would be convertible into EADS shares after about five years.

The police in Tbilisi, the capital of Georgia, were on alert Friday after an impromptu demonstration led to clashes on Thursday night between protesters and riot police along the city's main avenue.

The leaders of political parties opposed to President Mikheil Saakashvili called for more protests, and they accused Mr. Saakashvili of lurching toward centralized rule. Their calls occurred as the Georgian Parliament erupted in a public fistfight between members of rival political parties arguing in part over an unrelated law.

The unruliness demonstrated the degree of instability still prevalent in Georgia, which is weakened by an underdeveloped economy and years of corruption and disrepair. Mr. Saakashvili's promises of reform and increased democracy helped elevate him to the presidency in November 2003 at the front of a popular, nonviolent uprising against President Eduard A. Shevardnadze. The protests began Thursday after two popular wrestlers were sentenced to three months incarceration for extortion. Their supporters promptly vandalized the courtroom and began to demonstrate outside, blocking Rustaveli Avenue, where the protest grew and all traffic was stopped.

When negotiations between the police and protesters to open the avenue failed, officers, some with clubs, forced the demonstrators to the sidewalks and arrested at least 15 of them, said Guram Donadze, spokesman for the Interior Ministry.

Video played repeatedly on national television in Russia, which has strained relations with Georgia, showed Georgian police officers in riot gear beating demonstrators and stuffing them into police cars.

Seven police officers were injured, Mr. Donadze said. Opposition leaders said as many as 70 people were arrested, according to reports by news agencies.

The unrest continued Friday in the Georgian Parliament, which this week has debated a proposed election law stipulating that the mayor of Tbilisi will be elected by members of the City Council and not by a direct vote, as many Georgians have expected since Mr. Saakashvili began pledging to make the country more democratic. The mayor is currently appointed.

The day's Parliament session descended into bedlam as members exchanged shoves and punches, and the meeting was adjourned.

Giorgi Baramidze, the minister of European and Euro-Atlantic integration, played down the protests and predicted they would be conducted peacefully.

''It is a normal thing in democratic countries,'' he said in a telephone interview. ''We don't block demonstrations. They want to protest against it, and they have a full right to do it.''

He said the previous demonstration was broken up because the protesters illegally blocked traffic for two hours.

Senator Harry Reid of Nevada, the Democratic leader in the Senate, apologized Thursday to 33 Republican colleagues for a document distributed by his office that listed contributions that some of them received from the lobbyist Jack Abramoff along with critical news reports on their past actions and statements.

''I am writing to apologize for the tone of this document and the decision to single out individual senators for criticism in it,'' Mr. Reid said after the memorandum, headed ''Republican Abuse of Power,'' drew criticism from some Republicans. ''As you know, I myself have been the subject of similar personal attacks from Republican outlets. I understand the unfair picture they can paint and the pain they can cause.''

Mr. Reid has been harsh in his attacks this week on what he describes as a Republican culture of corruption exposed by Mr. Abramoff's recent guilty plea to bribery charges -- even drawing comparisons between Republicans and organized crime.

And Democrats have been aggressively working to tie Republicans to the scandal and make it a top 2006 campaign issue. But Republicans, including the office of Senator Bill Frist of Tennessee, the majority leader, cried foul over the 25-page document that attacked individual senators for the contributions and for other acts placed under the headings of ''Putting K Street Before Main Street'' and ''Out of Touch.'' They said the document was a blatantly political effort produced with taxpayer money in Mr. Reid's Senate leadership office.

He and fellow Democrats did continue to press Republicans on their Abramoff ties on Thursday, however, sending letters to Vice President Dick Cheney and 20 cabinet secretaries and agency heads asking them to disclose any dealings they had with the lobbyist.

The Internal Revenue Service has suspended at least eight workers in the Chicago area in a criminal investigation into bribery and other offenses, union officials and colleagues of the workers said.

The suspensions came after agents of the Treasury Department's inspector general for tax administration made predawn visits to the homes of at least five I.R.S. employees on June 22, urging them to cooperate with the investigation, said Charlie Turek, president of the National Treasury Employees Union local in Chicago.

Mr. Turek and lawyers familiar with the case said a federal grand jury was expected to hand up indictments, in what would be the first major corruption case brought against a group of I.R.S. workers since Congress passed the I.R.S. Reform and Restructuring Act of 1998.

''I am sure the inspector general will indict as many as he can,'' Mr. Turek said.

David C. Williams, the inspector general, declined comment.

Those under investigation include an appeals officer, two tax collectors and an auditor.

In one case an I.R.S. worker and a tax professional were taped discussing a $25,000 fee to fix a tax case, people who have heard the tape said.

One of the tax collectors was caught on tape agreeing to take money in return for reclassifying an overdue tax bill as currently not collectible.

While some of the taping was done by informers who agreed to wear recording devices after they were presented with evidence of their role in crimes, tape recorders were also placed at customer service counters.

As many as eight I.R.S. workers at four Chicago offices were suspended with pay three weeks ago and were told that they would be fired, colleagues said.

In addition to the workers facing criminal charges, a number of I.R.S. workers at four Chicago offices are expected to be disciplined for failing to report efforts to bribe them since the investigation began in 1998, colleagues and other people who are familiar with the case said.

The investigation also uncovered evidence that at least one I.R.S. auditor had been paid to prepare tax returns, which were signed by one of the tax professionals. Federal rules prohibit I.R.S. employees from preparing tax returns for pay.
